Key Facts Contracts More than 1,051 contracts were signed in the current budget year under the public media system.

What the contract review covers

On 17 August 2026, a MinTIC statement following an extraordinary board meeting on 15 August disclosed the contract numbers. The statement came from the new administration of the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia, which operates as Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC.

The statement said the contracts were signed in the current budget year. The total value is more than COP 100,000 million, which equals about US$32 million.

Between 6 and 7 August 2026, 87 contracts were signed for approximately COP 4,000 million. That is about US$1.3 million.

All of these processes will be subject to review as part of the reorganisation announced by the new management of Inravision. The review aims to check how the contracts were awarded.

The reorganisation began on 7 August, right after the news programming strand, the franja informativa, ended on 6 August.

Understanding the institutional names

The organisation formerly called RTVC Sistema de Medios Publicos is now Inravision Sistema de Medios Publicos. RTVC announced in April 2026 that it was taking back its historic name.

Write it as ‘Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC’.

The new gerente — general manager — is Angela Maria Mora Soto, a lawyer appointed by the government of Abelardo De la Espriella. She replaces Hollman Morris.

The ICT minister is Alexandra Falla.

Do not assume these 1,051 contracts belong solely to RTVC. The reporting groups them under the public media system umbrella.

This difference matters for investors and professionals who follow government contracts. The legal entity in charge of each contract can change.

Why the review matters now

President Abelardo De la Espriella took office on 7 August 2026.

The contract review is part of a wider reorganisation of public media. This may lead to new buying rules or the ending of some contracts.

For businesses that work with public broadcasters, this review creates uncertainty. Existing contracts may be delayed or renegotiated.

The review also shows how the new administration wants to spend public money. They will look closely at contracts signed by the previous government.

What happens next

The new management has not said when the review will finish. They have said all processes will be checked during the restructuring.

No contracts have been cancelled or suspended so far. The review is still in its early stages.

Watch for news from Inravision about findings or changes. The government may also release new rules for contracts.

For now, this is a review, not a cancellation. Contract holders should watch for updates and keep their documents ready.

This review is part of a larger effort by the De la Espriella government to change state agencies. The pension reform and diplomatic appointments are also being looked at.

Vilma Velasquez, Colombia’s ambassador to Haiti, is under investigation by the foreign ministry. The issue is about US$500,000 in unexplained transfers, including a cheque from the embassy’s operating account to her personal account.

This was reported on 7 August 2026. She denies the claim, saying 500,000 dollars never came in.

She was already suspended by the Procuraduria in May 2026 for backing Ivan Cepeda in politics.

The Constitutional Court may send the pension reform back to Congress again. This would be the second time.

The plans for savers and for moving funds to Colpensiones are still being discussed.

The total amount is about COP 25 billones, which is close to 25 trillion Colombian pesos. That is about US$8 billion.

These actions share a common idea: the new government is taking more control over institutions and contracts. Investors should expect more reviews and possible changes in policy.

Broader context for investors

Vilma Velasquez, Colombia’s ambassador to Haiti, is under investigation by the foreign ministry over about US$500,000 in unjustified transfers, including a cheque from the embassy’s operating account to her personal account. This came out on 7 August 2026. She denies it, saying 500,000 dollars never came in. She had already been suspended by the Procuraduria in May 2026 for political participation, for backing Ivan Cepeda.

What is the total value of the contracts? The total value exceeds COP 100,000 million, which is about US$32 million. An additional 87 contracts signed in early August are worth about COP 4,000 million (US$1.3 million). Are these contracts being cancelled? No. They are under review as part of a reorganisation. No cancellations have been announced so far. Which entity signed these contracts? The reporting refers to the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia and Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC. The figures cover the public media system.

World.title: A Week On, Colombia’s Quake Toll Is Still Moving
World.content:
Colombia · Disaster

Key Facts The toll As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut, 287 people are dead. Also, 4,147 are injured, 194 are still missing, and 355 were rescued.

As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut, 287 people are dead. Also, 4,147 are injured, 194 are still missing, and 355 were rescued. The damage The disaster destroyed 26,392 homes and damaged 127,608 more. In total, 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments.

The disaster destroyed 26,392 homes and damaged 127,608 more. In total, 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments. The reach The event affected 185,996 people and 120,671 families. It also hit 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads.

The event affected 185,996 people and 120,671 families. It also hit 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads. Numbers move both ways The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight, because duplicates get removed as names are confirmed.

The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight, because duplicates get removed as names are confirmed. A private cheque David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million, which is about US$32 million, towards reconstruction.

David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million, which is about US$32 million, towards reconstruction. The politics A censure motion against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán was announced on 17 August. This happened because of photographs of him on the beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

Seven days after a magnitude 7.4 quake hit Chocó, the official count is still being revised in both directions — and the politics has arrived.

If you have been trying to follow Colombia’s earthquake from abroad, the hardest part is that the numbers keep changing. A week after the magnitude 7.4 quake struck on 10 August, centred five kilometres south of San José del Palmar in Chocó, the official toll has gone up and then back down. Here is where it actually stood at the last full count, and what has happened around it since.

President Abelardo De la Espriella announced the Nubank founder’s donation. A censure motion against the housing minister followed. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Where the count stands

The national disaster agency, UNGRD, gives updates from time to time, not live numbers. Its last full count, at 18:30 on 16 August, showed 287 dead and 4,147 injured.

Another 194 people are still missing. Also, 355 have been pulled out alive.

Watch these two numbers because the gap between them shows where the toll will change next. The damage is huge for a country this size.

26,392 homes were destroyed. 127,608 were damaged, and 197 buildings fell.

Damage hit 472 municipalities across 15 departments. Public buildings also suffered: 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads were affected.

On 15 August, the official figure was 294. On 16 August, it was 287.

A falling toll can look scary if you have not seen it before, so here is why. In the first days after a disaster, the same person may be counted more than once.

For example, one count may come from a town, another from a hospital, and another from a rescue team. As names get confirmed, duplicate counts are removed.

For anyone watching from far away, write down the time and date for every number you see. A figure without a date is not very useful this week.

This is the mistake most news reports make. On 12 August, the governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi, said the search and rescue phase was over in her area.

She said they were no longer looking for people under the rubble.

Why the death toll went down

The search is over in Chocó, not nationally

That rule applies only to Chocó. The national emergency is still active, because 194 people remain missing.

So reports that Colombia has stopped searching are only partly correct. Chocó has moved to rebuilding, but other areas have not.

Money, tolls and a minister at the beach

David Vélez, founder and leader of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million — about US$32 million — for reconstruction. He confirmed this himself after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced it.

The road agency ANI, led by president Ricardo Ayerbe, has removed tolls, but less widely than news suggests. The waiver covers trucks with heavy machines, emergency gear, and aid supplies, on specific roads only.

Those roads are Buga–Buenaventura, Malla Vial del Valle, Armenia–Pereira–Manizales, Tercer Carril Bogotá–Girardot, and Girardot–Ibagué–Cajamarca. Fines for overloaded trucks are paused, so aid vehicles are not penalised.

Private car drivers still pay.

Politics has entered too. On 17 August, a censure motion was announced against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán, due to photos of him at a beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

It is announced, but not yet voted on.

What this means if you live in or invest in the region

Housing will shape the coming two years. With 26,392 homes destroyed and 127,608 damaged, this becomes a rebuilding and money story long after rescue work ends.

The roads on ANI’s list are the same ones used for cargo between Buenaventura, Colombia’s main Pacific port, and the inland areas. Businesses moving goods through that port should check ANI notices, not general headlines.

The Vélez donation matters for another reason. US$32 million from one private person is a big part of the early rebuilding costs.

This amount sets a new level for other big Colombian companies to compare with.

The censure motion shows how fast disaster aid turns into politics in this country. If you have projects waiting for housing-ministry decisions, this is a delay risk you should plan for.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people died in Colombia’s earthquake? The national disaster agency UNGRD recorded 287 deaths in its cut at 18:30 on 16 August 2026, with 4,147 injured and 194 people still missing. The figure moves between cuts, so always check the date attached to it. Why did the death toll go down? It was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Early counts often double-record the same victim through different channels, and duplicates are removed as identities are confirmed. Has the search for survivors ended? In Chocó, yes — the governor declared the search and rescue phase over on 12 August. Nationally it remains open, with 194 people still unaccounted for. Are Colombia’s toll roads free after the earthquake? Only for specific vehicles. ANI has exempted vehicles carrying heavy machinery, emergency equipment and humanitarian aid on a defined list of corridors, and suspended overload fines. Private cars still pay.

World.title: Peru’s Mining Boom: Investment Up 42.7%, Not 74%
World.content:
Peru · Mining

Key Facts Investment rise Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina.

Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina. The 74% myth A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total.

A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total. Top spenders Leading investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%).

Leading investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%). Company profits MMG (which runs Las Bambas in Peru) reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%—not 141%, which is the rise in cash.

MMG (which runs Las Bambas in Peru) reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%—not 141%, which is the rise in cash. Quellaveco shines Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine brought in US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion a year earlier.

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine brought in US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion a year earlier. Copper giant Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m).

Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m). Weak spot Exploration spending rose only 1.3%, to US$336.4 million, even as investment boomed.

The real story: Peru’s mining investment hit US$3.3 billion in H1 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. That 74% figure? It’s a Mexican miner’s revenue.

If you’ve seen headlines about Peru’s mining sector surging 74%, you might be forgiven for thinking the country is swimming in cash. But the actual official figure is different: mining investment rose 42.7% to US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) via state news agency Andina. The 74% bump belongs to Fresnillo, a Mexico-only miner—not Peru. Let’s clear up the confusion so you know what’s really happening on the ground.

An open-pit operation in the Peruvian Andes. Mining investment reached US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The real numbers from MINEM

Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) says mining investment reached US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026. That is 42.7% more than the US$2.3152 billion from the same time last year.

This is the official total for the whole mining sector. It shows steady growth, but not the 74% jump that some headlines mention.

MINEM lists the top investors as Southern Peru, Shougang Hierro Peru, Las Bambas, Antamina, Buenaventura, and Cerro Verde. Southern Peru alone spent US$432.7 million, which is 101.1% above a year ago.

Exploration spending is the weak part. It rose only 1.3%, reaching US$336.4 million.

Investment is strong, but finding new mineral deposits is slow. For comparison, US$3.304 billion equals about 11.1 billion soles, using the rate of 3.3647 soles per US dollar.

This healthy number shows mining firms are confident and spending on projects. That is important because Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer.

The 74% figure is real, but it does not apply to Peru. It comes from Fresnillo, a mining company based in Mexico, whose first-half 2026 revenue rose 74.7% to US$3.38 billion.

Fresnillo also reported a net profit of US$1.46 billion, up 213%. But it has no mines in Peru—its operations are at Saucito, Herradura, Juanicipio, Fresnillo, Cienega, and San Julian.

That 74% figure does not reflect Peru’s mining health. If you see such claims, check the source carefully.

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine in Peru earned US$2.161 billion in revenue. That is up from US$1.524 billion in H1 2025, a 41.8% increase.

Higher copper prices and output helped the rise. Production was slightly lower, but the result still improved.

The official Peruvian number is the 42.7% investment rise. Trust that one instead.

Why does this matter? Investment shows what companies plan for the future.

Profits can change quickly, but spending signals long-term confidence.

The confusion likely comes from mixing company results with sector data. For example, MMG’s profit jumped, but that is just one firm, not all miners.

Fresnillo’s revenue growth is big, but it belongs to a different country. Peru-linked miners still had a strong first half, even if the 74% headline is wrong.

MMG, which runs the Las Bambas copper mine in Peru, reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%. Profit for equity holders was US$897.2 million.

Some say 141% growth, but that number is for cash, not earnings. Las Bambas drove the result, and MMG called it its best financial performance in over ten years.

Southern Copper, which operates major mines in Peru, posted first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%. Its second quarter alone brought in US$4,289.0 million.

Where the 74% figure really comes from

Company-level wins that tell the real story

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine in Peru generated US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion in H1 2025. That’s a 41.8% increase, driven by higher copper prices and production—even though output was slightly lower. Southern Copper, which runs major mines in Peru, posted first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%; the second quarter alone was US$4,289.0 million.

Buenaventura, a Peruvian miner, saw net income attributable of US$514.0 million on H1 revenue of US$1,153.6 million, both clearly higher than the same period in 2025. Nexa Resources’ Peru subsidiary, Nexa Resources Peru S.A.A., reported US$669 million in revenue, up 45%—not the group.

The Nexa group’s first-half revenue was US$1,796 million, up 34%.

Why this matters for you

If you’re invested in Latin America, these numbers matter because they show where capital is flowing. Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer, and rising investment means more supply coming online—which could affect global copper prices and your portfolio.

For instance, MMG’s record profit and Southern Copper’s revenue surge are signals that copper demand remains strong.

For expats living in Peru, a mining boom often translates into more jobs, stronger local economies in mining regions, and a firmer sol. The currency has been stable, with the exchange rate around 3.36 soles per US dollar.

Mining investment also supports infrastructure and local businesses, from equipment suppliers to service providers.

But don’t get caught up in the hype. The 74% figure is a classic example of a number being taken out of context. Stick to the official MINEM data, and you’ll have a clearer picture of what’s actually happening. And if you’re watching specific stocks, remember that company-level results can vary widely—so look at each miner’s own numbers, not just the sector headline. Also, note that Peru’s energy and mines minister is Guillermo Shinno Huamani, sworn in in late July 2026 under President Keiko Fujimori—his office is the source for the official investment data.

Frequently Asked Questions

Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) reported mining investment of US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. Where does the 74% figure come from? The 74% figure is actually Fresnillo’s revenue growth—up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion. Fresnillo is a Mexico-only miner, not a Peru-specific metric. Which companies led mining investment in Peru? According to MINEM, the top investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%). How did Peru-linked miners perform in H1 2026? MMG’s Las Bambas contributed to a US$1,366.0 million profit after tax, up 89%. Anglo American’s Quellaveco saw US$2.161 billion in revenue. Southern Copper reported first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%.

World.title: Mexico’s Military Service Draw: Who the 2026 Lottery Covers
World.content:
Mexico · Explainer

Key Facts Lottery date: The Servicio Militar Nacional (SMN) draft lottery for Clase 2008 — men turning 18 in 2026 — is set for November 2026, according to SEDENA official information. The exact day hasn’t been published.

The Servicio Militar Nacional (SMN) draft lottery for Clase 2008 — men turning 18 in 2026 — is set for November 2026, according to SEDENA official information. The exact day hasn’t been published. Who is drawn: The main class is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year, plus ‘remisos’ — men who missed registering when they should have. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ (you serve) or a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’ (standby).

The main class is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year, plus ‘remisos’ — men who missed registering when they should have. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ (you serve) or a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’ (standby). 18–39 range: That age bracket exists only because the law’s obligations run to 31 December of the year a man turns 40. ‘Remisos’ — men who never registered — can be anywhere in that range. It’s not a new conscription band.

That age bracket exists only because the law’s obligations run to 31 December of the year a man turns 40. ‘Remisos’ — men who never registered — can be anywhere in that range. It’s not a new conscription band. Registration windows: The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries in the second half of the year a man turns 18. The 2026 convocatoria opens the municipal window from 2 January to 15 October 2026.

The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries in the second half of the year a man turns 18. The 2026 convocatoria opens the municipal window from 2 January to 15 October 2026. Cartilla liberation: The cartilla (military ID card) is liberated in December 2026. Those assigned ‘encuadrado’ attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027.

The cartilla (military ID card) is liberated in December 2026. Those assigned ‘encuadrado’ attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027. Voluntary for women: Women have been able to take part voluntarily since 2000 and are not subject to encuadramiento.

Women have been able to take part voluntarily since 2000 and are not subject to encuadramiento. Beyond the law: Claims that everyone aged 18 to 39 will be integrated into the Army if drawn go beyond what the law and SEDENA explicitly state. Treat them with caution.

The November draft lottery has a clear target group — and it isn’t everyone aged 18 to 39.

If you’ve seen posts claiming Mexico is about to draft everyone aged 18 to 39 into the Army, take a breath. Nothing changed this month. The claim doing the rounds is recycled coverage of SEDENA’s January 2026 convocatoria — the routine annual cycle being reported as news.

Mexico’s military service draw is held in November. No new rule was announced in August. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
