World.title: Peaceful return of Abkhazia: opposition leader Nika Gvaramia’s vision for Georgia’s policy
World.content:
Peaceful return of Abkhazia to Georgia

The Abkhaz conflict could be resolved not through war or discussions about the past, but through Georgia‘s European integration, economic development and shared security interests. Opposition politician Nika Gvaramia made the remarks in an interview with Formula television.

Gvaramia believes Georgia must overcome the trauma left by the war. At the same time, the country should become an attractive political and economic space for Abkhaz people.

He identifies EU membership, the development of the Anaklia port and a stronger Georgian role in the “Middle Corridor” as key elements of this strategy.

Gvaramia’s interview has already sparked public debate. Many viewers believe the politician moved beyond traditional rhetoric and proposed a rational and pragmatic approach to resolving the conflict, something rarely seen in Georgia’s political arena.

Personal memories of Sukhumi and Abkhazia’s strategic importance

Nika Gvaramia was 16 when he left Sukhumi. In an interview, he said he had lived in Tbilisi twice as long as he had lived in Sukhumi. Nevertheless, he still considers Sukhumi his home city.

For him, Abkhazia is both his homeland and a territory of particular strategic importance to Georgia. Gvaramia does not view the issue solely from the perspective of a displaced person.

He says Abkhazia’s geographical location, access to the Black Sea and economic potential distinguish this conflict from other conflicts in the post-Soviet space.

At the same time, he believes the 2008 war also demonstrated the strategic importance of the Tskhinvali region. The blockade of the country’s main transport route from that territory split Georgia in two and threatened links between the country’s eastern and western regions.

Nika Gvaramia

Gvaramia says that his experiences during the war and forced displacement made it difficult for him to look at the Abkhaz issue without emotion for a long time. He also recalls evidence of crimes committed in Abkhazia that he encountered while working at the prosecutor’s office.

However, he says that in recent years he has concluded that an approach based solely on trauma makes finding a solution impossible:

“Trauma is very important, it is part of historical memory… But traumatic memories are dangerous: they carry a threat, they act like a noose — they prevent us from moving forward and block development.”

Trauma, fear of war and government rhetoric

According to Gvaramia, Georgian Dream has turned the public trauma of war into a constant source of fear. As a result, the goal of restoring territorial integrity has given way to the attitude of “as long as there is no war”.

He said that for many years he himself approached the Abkhaz issue from a position of anger and intransigence. He considered dialogue with Abkhaz people impossible and saw the use of force as the solution. Later, he concluded that this approach was harmful to the country.

“Unfortunately, the actions of Georgian Dream have not led to the position that ‘this is my country, and I will fight to the end’. Instead, they have created the attitude: ‘I do not want war; there must be no war.'”

Gvaramia considers the desire to avoid war natural. People in Georgia have direct experience of the 2008 conflict: they watched the bombing of cities, the deaths of people and bombs falling on their country on live television.

However, he believes the problem arises when the government uses this experience as a tool of political control. Constant reminders of the threat of another war push people towards inaction instead of encouraging them to seek a solution to the problem.

In his view, Georgian society wants Abkhazia back, but not at the cost of war. Gvaramia believes politicians should take both sentiments into account at the same time.

“If we want to work with these people and consider ourselves politicians, we must understand that they also care about Abkhazia’s future, but they do not want war.”

According to Gvaramia, a military solution is unacceptable today not only because of public opinion. Georgia does not have the resources needed for such an approach, so statements about war that lack a realistic assessment of the country’s capabilities cannot form the basis of a responsible political plan.

He notes that the younger generation is gradually losing its emotional connection with Abkhazia and calls this one of the main challenges:

“Essentially, if we lose Abkhazia from our memory, that will also mean a real loss of the territory.”

In his view, over time, memories of the past alone will not be enough to preserve the idea of territorial integrity.

Pashinyan’s example and overcoming trauma

Gvaramia cites Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan as an example of a leader who managed to overcome the burden of traumatic historical memory. In his view, Pashinyan tried to separate the state’s future from historical and territorial claims.

In this context, Gvaramia discusses Armenia’s changing approach to issues related to Mount Ararat and Karabakh.

He believes the aim of this policy was to free Armenia from Russian influence and create new economic opportunities for the country:

“Such changes take decades, but Pashinyan achieved them in a very short time. He removed the image of Ararat from the official seal and said that it is part of our history, but not part of our geography.

If we want problems with Turkey, then yes, let’s continue depicting Ararat, but then we will remain poor and dependent on Russia. If we do not want that, then let’s reach an agreement and remove Ararat from the seal, because it is not actually in our territory.

Then our relations with both Turkey and Azerbaijan will improve. We will have more money, gain the prospect of moving towards the European Union and no longer be tied to Russia.”

At the same time, Gvaramia stresses the legal difference between Abkhazia and Karabakh. He notes that the international community recognises Abkhazia as Georgian territory, while Karabakh was not recognised as part of Armenia.

But for him, the main issue is not the status of these territories, but the political influence of traumatic memories and the possibility of breaking free from their grip.

The European Union as a magnet for Abkhazia

According to Gvaramia, the first step towards rapprochement with Abkhaz people should rest on mutual needs rather than rhetoric about mutual love. He believes such appeals do not reflect the reality that has emerged since the war, and that the truth is that Abkhaz and Georgian people do not feel affection for each other today:

“We are lying when we say that we are brothers… We do not love each other now; we cannot love people who kill our neighbours. But we should think about the fact that, at this moment, we need each other from a pragmatic point of view.”

At the same time, Gvaramia stresses that Abkhaz people do not have warm feelings towards Russians either:

“Abkhaz people are not a nation that loves Russians, and they never have been. There is a perfectly rational reason for that. Russians consider them second-class people, while Georgians do not — and Abkhaz people feel this very clearly.”

Gvaramia envisions a Georgia that has joined the EU as an attractive country for Abkhaz people. Such a state would offer access to European passports, freedom of movement, a developed economy and institutional guarantees protecting minority rights.

In his view, EU involvement would also create financial opportunities for rebuilding Abkhazia. Security guarantees, meanwhile, would come not from a Russian military presence but from international and European institutions.

Under this model, Abkhaz people should not become second-class citizens of Georgia. They should have full political and civil rights:

“We are offering Abkhaz people a good life — and is there any Abkhaz person who would refuse a good life? But we are not offering it at the cost of turning them into second-class people. No, they must be full citizens of Georgia.”

Gvaramia believes Georgians and Abkhaz people will need several decades to become accustomed to each other again. At the initial stage, mutually beneficial economic cooperation could form the basis of their relations.

Anaklia and the Middle Corridor

A key element of Gvaramia’s strategy is the deep-water port of Anaklia. He sees Anaklia as a potential economic “magnet” for Abkhazia.

Under his plan, Georgia should become an important link in the Middle Corridor, connecting Central Asia with the Black Sea. The route would connect Europe with the markets and resources of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and other countries in the region.

Gvaramia places particular emphasis on rare earth metals and lithium. In his view, the importance of these resources is growing, while Central Asian countries need an alternative route to Western markets because existing routes depend on Russia, China or Iran.

“The main thing for me is EU membership and developing the Middle Corridor. I use this word deliberately — development. We need to develop this route.”

In his view, Georgia should build the Anaklia port with Western capital, while American, British and European organisations should take part in its management. In that case, the port would become more than just an economic asset and could provide an additional security guarantee for Georgia:

“Nothing receives stronger protection from the Western world than property: not international treaties, not security commitments, not the charters of any alliances. No, property enjoys the greatest protection in any Western society.”

Gvaramia also believes Anaklia needs a democratic system of governance to develop. A major international investor will not pursue a long-term project in conditions of corruption and a lack of transparency.

That is why, in his view, a Western investor sees the port’s construction, European integration, democratisation and restoration of territorial integrity as parts of a single strategy.

Gvaramia believes the port of Ochamchire could also become part of this economic space in the future. This would make cooperation with Georgia serve Abkhazia’s economic interests.

Limits of compromise and a governance model

In the interview, Gvaramia says resolving the conflict will require concessions from both sides. However, he does not propose a specific model for future political governance.

The discussion touched on the experiences of Lebanon, Bosnia, Northern Ireland and Cyprus. Some of these examples show that allocating government positions and powers along ethnic lines can make state institutions ineffective.

Gvaramia does not rule out an agreement covering Abkhazia’s special legal status, the distribution of political powers, the return of displaced people and property issues:

“Reconciliation is impossible without concessions.”

At the same time, he noted that Georgia is a state recognised under international law. Therefore, creating a new state “from scratch” should not become a necessary condition for resolving the conflict.

Gvaramia sees the European Union as the key foundation for a possible agreement. In his view, the EU accession process could provide security guarantees for Abkhaz people while preserving the principle of Georgia’s territorial integrity.

Enguri HPP: cryptocurrency mining and corruption allegations

In the final part of the interview, Gvaramia discussed electricity supplies and cryptocurrency mining in Abkhazia. He made serious corruption allegations against the government and Bidzina Ivanishvili personally.

According to Gvaramia, a significant share of the electricity generated by the Enguri HPP goes to Abkhazia free of charge. However, he says a substantial portion of this resource goes not to meet people’s needs but to power cryptocurrency mining farms:

“They supply them with twice as much electricity as they need, yet they still face shortages. It is astonishing. Why? Because this electricity goes to crypto farms — to the ability to make money literally out of thin air.”

He alleges that this scheme benefits groups operating in Abkhazia’s de facto authorities, Russian interests and people linked to the Georgian government.

He also criticised possible fuel supplies to Abkhazia from Georgian-controlled territory. According to Gvaramia, it remains unclear how such shipments are documented, who pays for them and where exactly the fuel goes.

In his assessment, there is a risk that the fuel could serve the needs of Russian military infrastructure in Abkhazia. Gvaramia also considers the issue in the context of Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Tamta Mikeladze’s assessment: an important vision and unanswered questions

Tamta Mikeladze, head of the Centre for Social Justice, described the interview as an expression of a rational and pragmatic political vision. She said Gvaramia had moved beyond established political rhetoric on Abkhazia and linked the issue of territorial integrity to the country’s development strategy.

Mikeladze particularly highlights his comments on overcoming traumatic memories, rejecting the false choice between war and capitulation, the European Union’s appeal and the possible role of the Anaklia port in strengthening security.

In her view, an important part of the interview is the challenge it sets for the opposition: alongside criticising the government, it should offer the country a comprehensive alternative project.

Tamta Mikeladze

However, Mikeladze sees several problems with Gvaramia’s approach. The first is the possible overemphasis on economic interests.

She notes that in ethno-political conflicts, economic benefits do not always outweigh fears of losing one’s identity, nationalist narratives and the idea of independence.

Therefore, Tbilisi should offer solutions on protecting Abkhaz identity, language and political autonomy. A promise of prosperity alone will not be enough.

The second issue is the Russian factor. According to Mikeladze, Gvaramia’s model relies heavily on a weakening of Russia.

It remains unclear what would happen if Moscow maintained its influence and military bases in the region. Under such circumstances, economic appeal cannot replace alternative security guarantees.

The third issue concerns efforts to overcome trauma. Mikeladze notes that Pashinyan’s approach has caused serious divisions within Armenia.

Some sections of society see his policies not as overcoming trauma but as a national defeat. Such changes therefore require long-term democratic, social and cultural work with communities affected by the conflict.

The fourth issue concerns the model for sharing power. According to Mikeladze, this aspect has often undermined previous peacebuilding efforts. The political status of Abkhazia, its representation and the distribution of powers are therefore far from secondary details.

Despite these questions, Mikeladze considers the interview an important basis for public debate. She believes other politicians should also offer democratic, future-oriented alternatives rather than build their positions around the traumas and confrontation of the past.

She also calls on the media to exercise caution. According to Mikeladze, if Georgian Dream uses territorial integrity to justify political or economic interests, the opposition should provide a well-grounded response.

Mikeladze’s main message is that the debate on Abkhazia should no longer focus solely on memories of war, mutual accusations and general calls for reconciliation.

Public policy should answer difficult questions: how will Abkhaz identity be protected, who will guarantee security, how will power be shared, and under what conditions can a common political space be created?

Peaceful return of Abkhazia to Georgia

World.title: The future of Abkhazia: from preserving the language to building a civic nation. View from Abkhazia, video discussion
World.content:
Abkhaz language and civic nation

The editor of the newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, Inal Khashig, and political scientist Astamur Tania discuss the challenges and state policy regarding the Abkhazian language, the shift in historical narratives surrounding the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, as well as the necessity of building an inclusive civic nation for the sustainable future of Abkhazia.

Main theses and arguments:

Preservation and Development of the Abkhaz Language — The language issue is viewed as the foundation of national identity, requiring not merely electoral campaigns, but a long-term state program encompassing education, ideology, and administrative measures. Overcoming Formalism in Language Policy — Existing legislative initiatives and laws (such as the 2007 law) face implementation problems; there is a risk that successive delays and amendments will boil down to a formalistic approach without real results. Balance Between the State Language and Interethnic Harmony — Grace periods for non-Abkhaz citizens to master the Abkhazian language are aimed at preventing discrimination and fostering a unified civic platform under conditions of inevitable bilingualism (Abkhaz and Russian). Countering Historical Revisionism — Attempts to rewrite the history of the conflict are observed in the Georgian information space (including the promotion of the pseudoscientific “Ingorokva theory” and the interpretation of the 1992 war exclusively as Russian aggression), which relieves Georgia of responsibility and hinders a peaceful settlement. Abkhazia’s Agency and the Reduction of Hate Speech — Abkhazia emphasizes its status as an established nation and an active subject of relations; both sides acknowledge the destructiveness of “hate speech” in the media, as a resumption of the conflict would be catastrophic for everyone. Formation of a Civic Nation and the Rule of Law — The key challenge is the transition from ethnic self-awareness to an inclusive civic nation that unites all ethnic groups in Abkhazia on the basis of shared values, legal order, security, and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Hello, Chegemskaya Pravda is on the air. Today, we are going to speak again about the very same topics that concern our Abkhaz society. This prolonged discussion regarding the Abkhaz language, the standards of proficiency in this language, the state language for members of parliament. At the parliamentary hearings, the parliamentary committee rejected – that is, did not recommend – the draft constitutional amendments proposed by the president. But, nevertheless, legally this does not mean, as I understood, that the issue has been removed from the agenda; one way or another, it can be included in the agenda of the parliamentary session, even without this recommendation from the profile committee. Our guest today is Astamur Tania.

Astamur Tania: Good day.

Inal Khashig: Good day. Generally, what do you think about this whole situation that has arisen with these amendments to the constitutional law?

Astamur Tania: Here, the topic of the Abkhaz language is periodically raised in the form of certain information campaigns, usually during some pre-election period or in connection with certain events. It is also impossible to manage without information campaigns. It is necessary to sharpen public attention on this problem.

I hope that this information campaign will not have an independent significance of its own, but will transform into some programmatic actions. Because, probably, everyone understands—both supporters of one approach and supporters of the second approach—that in itself this decision means little. Because here it should still be about a state program.

This program is both educational and ideological, because much rests even on questions of self-awareness. Because it is clear that with the help of the Abkhaz language it is impossible to obtain the volume of information necessary to participate in any competition. So, there must be some other incentives. Just like that, in a natural way, unfortunately, it will not work.

These must be administrative measures and measures of an ideological nature. The Abkhaz language is inextricably linked with issues of identity. This is a big task on all fronts.

Now, regarding the presidential initiative specifically: to be honest, I consider it rational. Some argue that it involves an unequal approach, but I believe it is not aimed at discrimination.

On the contrary, its purpose is to address potential concerns so that advancing the Abkhaz language development program is not perceived as discriminatory by non-Abkhaz residents. After all, preserving interethnic harmony, maintaining consensus, and building a unified civic platform are fundamental for our society.

From this perspective, the approach is entirely sound. However, we must ensure this does not lead to endless postponements. The state must actively work on this by defining clear criteria in legislation to specify what constitutes fluency in the Abkhaz language.

This requirement should apply not only to the parliament but also to the executive branch. Implementing it within the judiciary will be more complex, as it requires extensive work to adapt the full body of legal terminology, which demands highly specialized legal expertise.

Inal Khashig: There are terminologies. All of that exists.

Astamur Tania: I know that preliminary work has been carried out—mostly at the level of compiling dictionaries of legal terms, as far as I am aware. However, implementation within the judiciary is far more difficult purely due to professional constraints.

That is why I believe the presidential initiative reflects today’s realities. It creates a space for compromise among political participants and allows us to develop proper criteria for assessing Abkhaz language proficiency.

If we fail to reach an agreement and leave everything as it is—which could easily happen if the president’s proposed law fails to pass—we will remain at a standstill. The entire process could degenerate into a formalistic routine, similar to what we witnessed during the presidential elections, and only spread further.

Therefore, as an initial step, I view this approach as very reasonable. Since there is no discrimination involved, I see no basis to claim it is unconstitutional.

Inal Khashig: I have my own perspective on this, though doubts constantly trouble me. The initiative grants a deferment to non-ethnic Abkhazians, but I am convinced that in five years, by 2032, we will find ourselves with the exact same results.

Astamur Tania: That certainly cannot be ruled out.

Inal Khashig: Indeed. But my concern is the formalistic approach toward the Abkhaz language itself. For instance, the language law was adopted in 2007 and was meant to take full effect in 2015, requiring the entire Abkhaz bureaucracy to be fluent in the state language.

Yet, even if a good half of them are fluent today, we should consider ourselves lucky—especially since no actual testing or measurements were ever conducted.

Astamur Tania: If at least a “bad half” had command of it.

Inal Khashig: Yes, yes. I am afraid that, strictly speaking, we will simply do this—formalize the commission itself, which we will bring to formal absurdity. Like, here is a good guy, he knows 10 words.

Astamur Tania: If we do not change our attitude toward our state, then in the Abkhaz language, and in security, and in the economy, we will have roughly the same result. You are right. This is a broader question than the Abkhaz language. It is just that now it is at the peak of relevance due to the debates in parliament and in society. In fact, this is a question of our attitude.

Various arguments are brought up that the quality of parliamentarism may drop from this. It seems to me that despite the absence of this norm, the quality of our parliamentarism was declining anyway. So the problem, after all, is not only in the Abkhaz language. This is a hackneyed phrase that we always get the government we deserve, that it is a reflection of our society. Therefore, this is a giant societal problem. But it must be dealt with.

First of all, the authorities, you see—to change the quality of authority, those in power must work on changing the quality of society as well. This goal must be set. Not simply to sit out one’s tenure in parliament or executive power. It is necessary to influence society, its enlightenment, its self-awareness, its creative potential. Therein lies the main task. Otherwise, you are right, it will drift on its own, like everything else.

Inal Khashig: It seems to me that the situation around the Abkhaz language is indeed much broader. It shows, probably, our attitude toward the law in general. This applies not only to the Abkhaz language.

We have passed very many all sorts of legislative acts, proper laws, but then we tried in every way to bypass them. An active advertising campaign is taking place on the internet: acquire Abkhaz real estate, and so forth. So many lances were broken over this law on apartments, and still they sell Abkhaz real estate to foreigners. It is possible, it can be acquired.

Astamur Tania: Yes, that is also—you know what the matter is? It is impossible to contain the onslaught; it can only be directed into some profitable channel. Of course, it is possible for some time to contain the natural course of events with prohibitions. But we must nevertheless forecast how we can direct these investments, where our weak zones are.

Simply sitting like a dog in the manger will not work. Therefore, we must understand how in this harsh reality—what is our place. Today one hole was plugged, in another place it tore open. We must have some clear program of action, at least for the short term.

This concerns the economy, security, foreign policy, everything. What I am saying is very banal, but unfortunately, we always have a reactive response to something, to already accomplished facts. Although it was not difficult to predict that the course of events was leading to this. And we live for today. If an individual person can live for today like that, the state should not live like that.

Inal Khashig: The state somehow manages to.

Astamur Tania: It should still plan its future, the society.

Inal Khashig: I would like to switch to another topic now. Periodically, we are reminded of the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, which continuously remains at a dead end. Last time, we discussed how Georgian perceptions of Abkhazia and the Abkhaz people have changed, particularly through the influence of Pavel Ingorokva’s theory, which took a strong hold in Georgian thought.

Shortly after our conversation, I watched an interview with the Georgian historian Tsurtsumia on a Georgian YouTube channel. He noted that Ingorokva’s theory is actually marginal and lacks official state support.

Nevertheless, just the day before yesterday, I came across a vividly animated video. It was set in Sukhumi on the embankment, depicting peaceful civilians in a setting reminiscent of 1992, when a Russian military aircraft suddenly swoops in and begins bombing. The people are shown fleeing the embankment, trying to escape by ship or heading into the mountains.

Astamur Tania: Those are slightly different scenes, probably. Maybe it is one pie, but different slices.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but you see, this is proceeding very actively – why I understood this is not only Ingorokva’s theory about who the Abkhaz are and what their origin is, but in Georgian society the understanding of what the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict was is changing very actively. And what happened 33 years ago, 34 years ago. How the war started.

According to this cartoon… A cartoon is a certain part of upbringing. It also has its own audience. Directed at a certain audience. At children. It is important for me to understand why the Georgians converted this conflict into a conflict not between Georgians and Abkhaz, but a certain conflict between Russia and Georgia.

Astamur Tania: That is completely understandable, as acknowledging it would require admitting responsibility for starting the armed conflict. By the way, Shevardnadze did admit this responsibility—and while he claimed Kitovani was to blame, Kitovani was not the Defense Minister of Russia, but of Georgia. Everyone remembers, and archival footage still shows, how this war began and how the local Georgian population reacted.

Acknowledging this would require erasing entire sections of history. Instead, there is an effort to reshape the narrative of 1992 and merge it with the events of 2008, framing everything around legislation and the narrative of post-2008 occupation. Yet, a detailed examination—including the report by the International Fact-Finding Commission led by Heidi Tagliavini—confirmed that responsibility for initiating military action in both instances lay with the Georgian side.

Naturally, there is a desire to obscure this in the media space to advance narratives about occupation, aiming to shape international opinion to justify a forceful resolution or delegitimize the Abkhazian state.

We must react to this. The fact that animated videos are being produced on this topic shows an intent to pass this worldview down to the next generation. If we carry such a perspective into the future, achieving a peaceful settlement or joint progress will be extremely difficult. This is why it is essential to present the fullest possible picture, starting with the factual timeline.

Regarding Zura Tsurtsumia’s comments: first, it is positive that Georgian-Abkhaz relations are being examined at a solid academic level, attempting to move beyond today’s propaganda clichés toward a historical assessment of the conflict’s roots.

However, claiming that Ingorokva’s theory is marginal ignores reality in the Georgian media landscape, where it remains the most widespread view on the origins of the Abkhazian people. While prominent Georgian scholars considered it pseudoscientific—such as Javakhishvili, who noted that ancient Adyghe tribes inhabited Western Georgia prior to the Kartvelians and recognized the Apsilals and Abasgs as direct ancestors of modern Abkhaz—these classical works are largely ignored by mainstream media.

Instead, hate speech dominates the discourse among commentators—and we must acknowledge that hate speech exists on the Abkhaz side as well. Neither side benefits from this.

Objectively, neither we nor Georgia have any interest in a renewed armed conflict, which would yield disastrous consequences for both. Some in Georgian society may assume their larger population makes it an easy victory, but that is far from reality. We cannot afford to trigger such a dangerous cycle.

Both sides are equally served by abandoning hate speech and language that demeans human dignity and belittles culture, especially given that all human cultures, including Abkhazian and Georgian, are products of historical interaction and symbiosis.

Finally, addressing Tsurtsumia’s assertion—which is not unique to him—that the Abkhaz nation was deliberately engineered by Soviet authorities to counter Georgia: while Soviet policies influenced the development of both the Georgian and Abkhazian nations in the late 19th and 20th centuries, it is vital to recognize that the Abkhaz national identity was not an artificial creation.

In fact, during the 1930s and 1940s, deliberate repressive measures were used in an effort to suppress the formation of the Abkhaz nation.

Inal Khashig: That was when schools were closed.

Astamur Tania: Schools were closed, and the destruction of the intelligentsia—the bearers of this very idea—took place at that time. This inflicted a serious trauma.

But one must understand that this process is accomplished. It is an accomplished fact. And in dialogue with the Abkhaz, everyone must proceed from the premise that this is not simply an ethnos, but a formed nation. With its own ideas about borders, policy, with its own national mythology. This is not always equal to history. Here there is a completely different approach.

As I once spoke with an Abkhaz, he said in his heart: why did Gurandukht, the daughter of the Abkhaz king, marry Gurgen, the ruler of Tao-Klarjeti? Since then, the unification of the Abkhaz state with the Georgian one began. That is the feudal era. It is an accomplished fact. We can only look at it like that. It sounds like a parody.

The same applies to this issue. It is closer to us. These are already accomplished facts. We must take them into account. Proceed from the fact that this is a given. Second, there were in fact certain inaccuracies there.

I do not want to delve into that now. In itself, this attempt to approach the understanding of the origins of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict with a cool head, using academic material—if this happens more or less regularly, in the same calm atmosphere, then it seems to me that both societies can win from this.

Inal Khashig: On the other hand, it seems to me, given that this seems to be a recent event—the war is relatively a historical event, only 30 years ago—nevertheless, judging by what I read in social networks, certain articles, certain speeches of politicians or experts…

Astamur Tania: Very much so.

Inal Khashig: I still see a lot of statements specifically adjusting to the political opportunism of the moment. If you remember, in the 80s, in the 90s after the war, what were we called? Abkhaz separatists. Now you practically do not hear this term.

Astamur Tania: By the way, they started calling us Abkhaz separatists back during the war, and before that—Gudauta separatists. Although during that period Abkhazia had not yet declared that it was ceasing any relations with Georgia and was not going to live with it within common borders.

In its time, on the initiative of Georgian figures, the process of all kinds of division began in Abkhazia. They separated the Georgian sector from the Abkhaz State University. Then they withdrew the football team. Then they withdrew the Georgian faction from the Supreme Council. They began to sit separately. That is, they apparently assumed that gradually they would somehow paralyze things. And here the question arises: who was the separatist?

And the same with this term. And, by the way, “Gudauta separatists”—later this very term migrated into the documents of the United Nations. And for some time after the end of the war, when our authorities were already located in Sukhumi, they continued to call us Gudauta separatists. I think for the Abzhua Abkhaz this is a bit offensive. Gudauta-Abzzua separatists would have been sound better.

Inal Khashig: But, nevertheless, this term somehow went out of circulation. And we have already been switched to the idea that Abkhazia is a territory occupied by Russia. And at the same time, as for the Abkhaz—let us leave aside those social networks where we generally came down from the mountains, according to the Georgian version—in official rhetoric nothing is said about us anymore.

Astamur Tania: “Came down from the mountains” is also quite amusing, because on most of the coast, based on climatic conditions and the unhealthiness of this climate, it was practically impossible to live permanently. Even if you open the press of, say, the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it is evident that the affluent portion of the residents of the city of Sukhumi left Sukhumi for the summer period. Precisely when there was the peak of this disease, people left for the foothills, because living here was a bit dangerous.

Inal Khashig: And the most prosperous ones lived there.

Astamur Tania: Generally, we have a perception as if in the Middle Ages communications in Abkhazia—this applies to everything, we are talking about Abkhazia—ran along the coast like that; there was the Ancient Roman railway running, next to it the Byzantine highway, but in reality all communications passed through the foothills and across the ridges. It was later, with the arrival of the Russian Empire, that this network of communications familiar to us began to develop. And psychologically we begin to tie our perception of the past to what had already taken shape in the 19th and 20th centuries. There was no railway at the beginning of the 20th century yet.

Inal Khashig: This highway that exists now.

Astamur Tania: For example, construction of the Black Sea railway continued in 1918 still. The Russian Empire no longer existed, but it was unclear what would happen. But they continued to build it in the Gagra region in 1918. And now it seems that it was always there.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, I tried to understand. Why do they depict Abkhaz who did not participate in this conflict, or played some secondary role in this Georgian-Abkhaz conflict? In the war that took place in 1992-1993.

Astamur Tania: A moment is omitted. What quantity of weapons was transferred to Georgia under the Tashkent Agreement on the eve of the conflict? The Russian authorities of that time were far from being, to put it mildly, pro-Abkhaz.

This is evident from everything. This is visible if one reads at least the transcript of September 3 of the meeting of Shevardnadze, Yeltsin, Ardzinba, representatives of the North Caucasus, representatives of our various parliamentary deputations. Not only should documents be studied, one should read the transcript.

But why did Georgia start armed conflicts? It received at its disposal several motor rifle and tank divisions of the Transcaucasus Military District. Therefore, in their joy, they thought that it would be possible to quickly finish this business.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, why am I saying all this—I read an interesting Georgian perspective on why this is happening, that Abkhaz are being excluded from this conflict, that through such an exclusion—and, say, when a certain image of the enemy is removed from the Abkhaz in this conflict, in this war, if the Abkhaz played a non-primary role, it means they are not enemies. There is a hypothetical possibility they retain that later at some point we will make peace with them.

Astamur Tania: That is very hypothetical. In my opinion, it is impossible to do that. Because how can one take a segment of a section of thinking and take something out of there… It seems to me this is very much a laboratory theory.

Inal Khashig: But this is laboratory on the one hand, and on the other hand the Abkhaz themselves have their own perception of the war.

Astamur Tania: To reiterate: those in Georgia who deal with the Georgian-Abkhaz settlement or seek to study this issue must start from the accomplished fact of the Abkhazian nation’s existence. A nation cannot be treated as a third-party observer—it is an active subject. We are an active subject in our relations with Georgia. Recognized or unrecognized, by our internal structure, we are a nation—with our own statehood and our own distinct perception of both the past and the future.

Our perspectives may not always align, but if we look at history honestly, our centuries-long—even thousand-year-old—relations with various Kartvelian peoples, primarily Megrelians, cannot simply be painted in black-and-white. History saw different periods, including feudal wars, which, it should be noted, occurred internally among those groups as well. There was continuous interaction, symbiosis, and movement back and forth. This is why we find Megrelian surnames in Abkhazia, Abkhaz surnames in Zugdidi, and why Gali in particular serves as a concentrated microcosm where everything is intertwined.

We, too, must draw important policy conclusions from this. But there must be a foundational understanding that if there is a real desire to settle our relations or develop a pragmatic approach—though I do not expect major breakthroughs given our disagreements—it starts with recognizing that a political nation has formed here. Its members are not solely ethnic Abkhazians, but all citizens of Abkhazia. We, too, must recognize this and move away from a narrow communal mindset.

Inal Khashig: But, by the way, it is present.

Astamur Tania: That is natural, because that is where it started. But we must nevertheless move in the direction of a civic nation.

Inal Khashig: Well yes, a political nation. This distinction is crucial because, unfortunately, many people’s perception of the Abkhazian situation and where we stand today was shaped back in Soviet times.

Astamur Tania: In fact, the post-Stalin Soviet period wasn’t all bad. Despite setbacks during that recovery process, it was unthinkable to express such vile ideas in writing back then.

Inal Khashig: My point is slightly different. In Soviet times, the Abkhaz struggle focused on ethnic rights—opening schools, theaters, literary journals, and universities—since few anticipated the collapse of the Soviet Union. The political nation back then was subsumed under the concept of the ‘Soviet people,’ right?

Astamur Tania: Well, ‘the Soviet people’ was an ideological construct, though autonomous frameworks did exist.

Inal Khashig: Yet today, some still take a fragmented approach, viewing society purely as separate ethnic groups—Abkhaz, Armenians, Russians, and so on—rather than…

Astamur Tania: You mean moving toward a unified civic nation?

Inal Khashig: Exactly. That is essential.

Astamur Tania: That requires active political education. Some processes occur naturally: living within the same state fosters shared views on security, peaceful development, and the necessity of an independent Abkhazia. However, we must establish clear criteria for this political nation to avoid repeating the mistakes made in Georgia during the Gamsakhurdia era. As a polyethnic society, we must embed protections that guarantee the survival of the Abkhaz people. Our fellow citizens understand this foundational principle.

That brings us back to language. Over time, our entire society must achieve sufficient command of the Abkhaz language for daily communication. Naturally, our society will remain bilingual due to demographic and geopolitical realities. This is why Russian is constitutionally designated alongside Abkhaz. But ‘alongside’ must not mean replacing Abkhaz. Striking this balance requires preserving the Abkhaz language while maintaining interethnic harmony. We should engage Abkhaz academic circles and draw on international experience—such as the major initiatives used to revive and preserve Welsh alongside English.

Ultimately, we need a sense of proportion in both domestic and foreign policy. Though emotions run high, avoiding extremes is vital. A population of our size can only survive through moderation and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Having come full circle, it seems clear that the survival and development of Abkhazia depend on building an inclusive civic nation that encompasses all ethnic groups residing here as citizens…

Astamur Tania: Including Georgians, of course.

Inal Khashig: …who would also command the state language.

Astamur Tania: Regarding the Gali district specifically, we must rethink our policy. We must acknowledge that regardless of how they identify ethnically, the residents there represent a native Megrelian-Georgian population, many with historical Abkhaz roots.

Inal Khashig: We can dedicate a separate conversation to that topic. But building a civic nation—governed by the rule of law and grounded in our constitutional language framework—is key to securing our future so that we aren’t constantly fearing our own disappearance.

Astamur Tania: Though I think we are destined to sound the alarm for many years to come!

Inal Khashig: Building a civic nation takes time and represents a broader movement toward a state governed by the rule of law.

Astamur Tania: To end on a reassuring note: perhaps artificial intelligence will solve all these problems for us!

Inal Khashig: I hope so! On that note, we will wrap up today’s broadcast. Today, Astamur Tania and I discussed the Abkhaz language, the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, and why these complex questions persist. Goodbye. Until new meetings. Thank you.

Astamur Tania: Thank you.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, people leave” – from a march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video blog
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Judges vs ordinary pensioners in Azerbaijan: what the law and figures show
World.content:
Judges and pensions in Azerbaijan

The pension of Azerbaijani judge Jahangir Yusifov was increased from 4,700 manat (around $2,765) to 7,500 manat (around $4,412) after he took the matter to court. Thanks to special pension rules, judges’ pensions can be dozens of times higher than the country’s average pension.

For comparison: the minimum labour pension in Azerbaijan is 320 manat (around $188).

When Baku Court of Appeal judge Jahangir Yusifov retired in 2025 at the age of 65, the State Social Protection Fund awarded him a monthly pension of 4,700 manat. That amount was equivalent to around 58% of his average monthly salary while serving as a judge.

Yusifov demanded that his pension be increased to 8,200 manat (around $4,824), arguing that he had worked all his life under difficult conditions, possessed special professional qualifications, and had been subject to a high level of responsibility.

The Baku Administrative Court upheld most of his claim, increasing his pension to around 7,500 manat. His request for additional financial assistance equal to 10% of his pension was rejected.

This is not the first such case. Other retired judges have filed similar claims, including Azad Majidov, Anvar Seyidov, Ulvi Mayilov and others. The courts have upheld all of the claims filed.

These cases clearly demonstrate how the special social protection mechanism provided for judges under Azerbaijani law is applied in practice.

Judges’ pension provisions

Under Article 109 of the Law “On Courts and Judges,” judges’ pensions are calculated according to special rules and depend on their length of service as a judge.

For those who have served as a judge for at least five years, the pension may be set at 45% of their average salary.

For between 5 and 10 years of service, an additional 2% is added to the 45% for each additional year.

For between 10 and 15 years of service, the pension is set at 55% of the average salary, plus 5% for each additional year, but cannot exceed 80% of the average salary.

Pension calculations also take into account pension capital and other allowances предусмотренные by law.

These higher percentage rates and additional benefits based on length of service provide judges with special pension conditions compared with other groups of the population.

Is it possible to live on a pension?

A judge’s pension of 7,500 manat (around $4,412) is 23 times higher than the minimum pension and 12–13 times higher than the average pension.

For comparison, the official subsistence minimum for a pensioner, regardless of profession, is 245 manat (around $145).

The average pension is significantly higher than this threshold. Nevertheless, it can be difficult for a single pensioner to maintain a stable standard of living solely on an average pension. Older people often need additional sources of income, such as employment, family support or targeted social assistance.

According to official statistics, as of April 1, 2026, more than 105,000 old-age pension recipients were still working.

But state officials, prosecutors and judges are provided with a fundamentally different level of social protection. Many people in Azerbaijan view this approach as a “double standard” enshrined in law. And when it comes to lawsuits filed by judges seeking higher pensions, public discussions often include comments along the lines of: “Apparently, even that wasn’t enough for the judges.”

News in Azerbaijan

World.title: Heavy rain floods streets, basements and metro stations in Tbilisi – video
World.content:
Heavy rain in Tbilisi

Following heavy rainfall overnight on 14 August, the Georgian capital was once again flooded. Tbilisi City Hall issued a statement on the situation, saying the intense rainfall had “caused certain problems”.

According to the city authorities, central districts were the worst affected. Private homes and basements were flooded, while a retaining wall at one residential property collapsed. Streets across the city and areas around several metro stations were also inundated.

Throughout the night, residents posted videos from different parts of the capital showing flooded streets and squares. Residents of one street in the city centre also blocked the road, calling for help in dealing with the damage.

Videos published by city residents:

“The heavy rainfall in the capital caused problems in all ten districts. Gravel and stones were washed onto roads. Our staff are carrying out clean-up work around the clock. The rain was particularly heavy in the Vake, Mtatsminda and Krtsanisi districts.

“More than 500 personnel and 30 pieces of equipment have been mobilised across all affected areas and are involved in the clean-up operation. The work will continue until all the problems have been fully resolved,” said Giorgi Papava, head of Tbilisi’s main municipal services operator, Tbilservice Group.

World.title: Stress-free Book Week costumes with a musical twist
World.content:
Across Australia, the Children's Book Week parade with its costume displays is a cherished and sometimes dreaded tradition for generations of parents and kids.

This year, there's a musical twist to the theme: Symphony of Stories.

We talk to musically inclined parents, an author and an ABC Classic presenter to get ideas on how your kids can take part in the Symphony of Stories.

They also share tips on how to take some of the stress out of Book Week costume crafting.

Choosing books about music

ABC Classic presenter Danielle McGrane reads stories to her children every night.

"It's part of the ritual of going to bed," McGrane says.

For families looking to embrace this year's Symphony of Stories theme, books inspired by music can offer both reading inspiration and costume ideas.

McGrane's collection includes stories inspired by classical music, such as Carnival of the Animals and The Planets, which she's currently reading with her child.

"The Planets is a book about young explorers going to all the different planets and there's a little button that can be pressed to play the music from Gustav Holst's The Planets," she says.

Book Week celebrates the simple joy of reading, says Danielle McGrane. (ABC Classic: Lucy Zee)

Musical storybooks can be a great way to introduce young children to different instruments and composers.

"I've been reading and playing Carnival of the Animals with my kids from quite a young age," McGrane says.

"There are so many book versions of this story. And what it does is give instruments like the cello or the tuba a personality that kids can relate to."

Other books, such as The Flying Orchestra, can show children that "music is a tool for emotional expression," McGrane says.

Books like these can provide simple inspiration for Symphony of Stories costumes.

McGrane has some tips for parents who are anxious about jazzing up their costume game: "Pick two costumes you feel you can achieve, and offer your child the choice between those two."

Whether you're dressing your child as an animal from Carnival of the Animals or an instrument from The Flying Orchestra, McGrane says "the important thing is to feel the link between the story and the music."

Choosing books with musical connections

Blue Mountains author Jodie McLeod feels differently about Book Week, depending on which hat she's wearing.

"As an author, I can't wait to share my love of books with schools and students, but as a parent, I'm nervous," she says.

One of McLeod's books, Leonard the Lyrebird, has been inspiring Book Week costumes since it was published in 2018.

McLeod has seen children dress up as lyrebirds, which are famed for their mimicking abilities and impressive performances in the Australian bush.

"They would be wearing greys and browns, carrying some feathers and props with musical notes," she shares.

Author and parent Jodie McLeod has mixed feelings about Book Week depending on which hat she's wearing. (Supplied: Jodie McLeod)

Those musical touches feel especially fitting because Leonard the Lyrebird has found a second life as a stage musical, joining a long tradition of books that have been adapted for new audiences, from Gumnut Babies to Matilda.

McLeod says the boundaries between books, theatre and screen adaptations have become increasingly blurred, opening up even more possibilities for Book Week costumes.

"Tim Minchin's Matilda, for example, has a lot of iconic grey and white school uniforms with ties and blazers, and there's a lot of gorgeous choreography in that musical."

McLeod says practicality and cooperation of her kids are the deciding factors for Book Week.

The Book Week parade also gives teachers a chance to rock their costumes. (Supplied: Jodie McLeod)

As a parent of older children on the cusp of their teenage years, she has to take their likes and dislikes into account.

"My children have never been very inclined to wear elaborate costumes to school," McLeod admits.

"The best costumes have been those where my kids can dress up mostly as themselves, but have some feature or prop that distinguishes them as a character from a book."

This approach might be handy for families learning a musical instrument, especially one that's easy to carry.

For parents who don't have the time, budget or enthusiasm for elaborate costume-making, McLeod points out there's another way to embrace this year's musical theme: "incorporate some singing and dancing into the Book Week parade".

Find musical elements in books you already have

Book Week is the highlight of Ballarat-based mum of four Deneale Deppeler's year.

"I do love dressing up as a way to express my creativity through Book Week," Deppeler says.

Book Week is the highlight of the year for Ballarat-based mum of four Deneale Deppeler. (Supplied: Deneale Deppeler)

She even organises a Book Week version of trick-or-treating on her street, called "Books n' Bon Bons".

"I get a lot of joy out of it, but I know not everybody will feel the same," she says.

Deppeler is strict about ensuring her children dress up as characters from books rather than "just any TV characters".

Deneale Deppeler loves a bit of ceremony and an occasion to dress up. (Supplied: Deneale Deppeler)

But Deppeler says getting on board with this year's Symphony of Stories theme is easier than parents might think.

"Music might not always be in the front seat of a storybook, but you'll often find musical elements hidden throughout stories, even if it's not the main thing."

That means parents don't have to start with an obviously musical book to embrace the theme.

Deppeler points to popular favourites including Grug, Peter Rabbit, Paddington Bear and Ruby Red Shoes as potential sources of inspiration.

To keep Book Week as stress-free as possible, Deppeler has a few costume-making rules of her own, including deciding what costumes her kids will wear.

The aim is to create costumes using materials already in the house and items from her children's wardrobes.

Some of the examples Deppeler suggests include making cardboard cut-outs of a violin, or using a paper towel roll to create a clarinet or a microphone.

"This is where my creativity comes in," Deppeler says. "I just need a shoe box and some folding paper and bam, I've got an accordion; a Milo tin makes a drum."

Deppeler creates costumes mainly using items from around the house and her children's wardrobes. (Supplied: Deneale Deppeler)

Many popular children's stories, including Grug, feature musical elements between its pages. (Supplied: Deneale Deppeler)

Deppeler also recommends reusing costumes from previous Book Week parades.

"If you've got a bear costume from Paddington Bear, there's no reason why you shouldn't reuse it for stories like The Very Noisy Bear, which is about trying out different musical instruments," she says.

Ultimately, Deppeler says the most important thing about Book Week is "getting kids to become passionate about reading and discovering what other people are reading through their costumes."

ABC Classic celebrates Children's Book Week from Saturday 22 — Friday 28 August, exploring the connection between literature, imagination and classical music.
