World.title: Hockeyroos downed by reigning champions in World Cup pool match
World.content:
The Hockeyroos have been beaten by the Netherlands in their second match of the FIH Hockey World Cup, going down 4-2 despite a battling performance against the reigning champions.

Australia are nevertheless well placed to qualify for the second round with the group's other result going their way.

Rejuvenated Hockeyroos and Kookaburras tackle World Cup with fresh perspectives The Kookaburras and Hockeyroos' last major tournament was Paris 2024 where they exited in the quarter-finals. They have both experienced significant change since then, and are determined to start their new eras with success at the World Cup.

The Aussies took Monday's game to their hosts from the opening whistle in the Amsterdam suburb of Amstelveen, producing a strong first quarter and putting the world number one team under sustained pressure.

The Hockeyroos earned a startling eight penalty corners in the opening term, including seven in succession, but were unable to find the breakthrough.

Australia paid for their profligacy as the Dutch showed them how it is done, scoring with their first penalty corner through Yibbi Jansen in the 13th minute.

The Netherlands doubled their advantage in contentious circumstances.

Australia referred Joosje Burg's goal for a potential back stick in the build-up, with replays showing the ball had made contact with the back of a Dutch stick. However, because the incident occurred outside the attacking 23-metre area, it was deemed non-referable, and the goal stood.

Refusing to let the setback halt their momentum, the Hockeyroos continued to attack and were eventually rewarded through Steph Kershaw, who found the back of the net in the 23rd minute to reduce the deficit.

Kershaw was involved again as Australia drew level at 2-2, getting the faintest of touches on an Abi Williams flick to set up a thrilling finish against the tournament favourites.

With the match in the balance heading into the final quarter, the Netherlands showed why they are the world's top-ranked side.

The Dutch piled pressure on the Australian defence, earning five penalty corners in the final quarter, scoring twice in the space of four minutes through Burg and Marjin Veen to take control of Group A.

The Hockeyroos now turn their attention to Chile on Wednesday from 5:30pm, AEST.

Chile are pointless having lost 3-0 to Japan.

With Australia beating Japan 2-0 in their opening game, a Hockeyroos victory will ensure their progress to the next stage, unless Japan unexpectedly beat the Dutch. In that case, goal difference will come into play so Australia will be seeking a large win over the South Americans.

AAP

World.title: Swans coach 'disappointed' over Melbourne incident
World.content:
Sydney Swans coach Dean Cox says he is "disappointed" regarding allegations of sexual assault involving several players in Melbourne on Sunday night and that the club will have more to say on the issue today.

Police are continuing to investigate the alleged incident at the Pullman Hotel near the MCG, where the Swans were staying following their 36-point win over Essendon.

Victoria Police issued a statement on Monday saying detectives were investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne.

"The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning," a spokesperson said.

"The exact circumstances are yet to be established, and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing."

Police were investigating the alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel in east Melbourne. (ABC News)

On Tuesday morning, Cox spoke briefly to the media outside the Swans' headquarters in Sydney.

"Obviously extremely disappointed with what's happened and we understand there are questions and we'll update as we gather more information," he said.

Cox said it was too early to say whether the players involved would face sanctions from the AFL.

"We're working our way through everything with the AFL and the relevant parties and we'll update when we get more information," he said.

He said he had not yet spoken to the players but would do so "as the day unfolds".

Matthew Pavlich says the club is looking into what happened in Melbourne.

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich said on Monday that the club was still piecing together what happened in Melbourne and was undertaking its own internal inquiries.

"Safe to say, we're extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation," he said.

"We understand the level of interest in the matter, and there's going to be lots of speculation, but given it's a police matter right now, that's all that we can say."

The AFL is yet to comment beyond the brief statement the organisation released yesterday.

"The club made the AFL aware of the matter which is currently under Victoria Police investigation," the statement read.

World.title: Fungi fans celebrate its recognition as nature's third living kingdom
World.content:
Mycelium would not know or care if it was recognised by the Australian Labor Party.

Its priority over millions of years has been to work underground in ways that scientists are only beginning to appreciate.

But the ALP has a soft spot for mycelium, and all other forms of fungi.

At its recent national conference, federal Environment Minister Murray Watt explicitly recognised fungi as part of Australia's natural environment and biodiversity, separate and equal to flora and fauna.

"Fungi are vital to our ecosystem, and it is crucial that our environmental and biodiversity frameworks reflect this," Senator Watt told the conference.

Australia has as many as 250,000 fungal species. (Supplied: Stephen Axford)

The recognition follows years of advocacy by mycologists, biologists, ecologists and Australian citizen-scientist organisation Fungimap.

They are part of a global network of fungi fans celebrating the recent addition of the word "funga" to the Cambridge Dictionary to describe the third kingdom of living things.

FUNGA noun [u] biology, environment specialized All the fungi (=organisms that usually grow on and get their food from decaying material or other living things) that grow in a particular area or a particular period in time ~ Cambridge Dictionary

Fungimap committee member Catherine Marciniak, a grassroots ALP member of the Ballina branch in northern New South Wales, was one of the driving forces behind the party's recognition of fungi in its national platform.

Delicate species of fungi grow side-by-side. (Supplied: Catherine Marciniak)

The revised national platform commits Labor to conserving and restoring "flora, fauna, fungi, oceans and waterways", and could potentially lead to an amendment to the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act.

Ms Marciniak said recognition meant fungi would be included in biodiversity assessments, environmental planning, threatened species monitoring and research opportunities.

"Our concern was, if it's invisible, then it's not measured, and if it's not measured, it's not conserved," she said.

"For instance, we have a critically endangered rainforest right on our doorstep here … [that] has been surveyed for plants and animals, it's been surveyed for butterflies, but it's never been surveyed for a whole kingdom of life.

" We have no endangered species listed for fungi, which is madness. "

Stephen Axford and Catherine Marciniak are behind the push for fungi recognition. (Supplied: Planet Fungi)

Michael Priest, a former mycologist with the NSW Department of Primary Industries and Fungimap president, said fungi played a vital role in recycling nutrients, building healthy soils, carbon storage and supporting the health of up to 95 per cent of the Earth's trees.

Michael Priest says fungi form at least a third of all living things. (Supplied: Michael Priest)

"They underpin everything that we know of what's going on in our ecosystem," he said.

Dr Priest said with about 250,000 species of fungi in Australia and only about 12,000 formally described, there was still much to learn, including potential industrial and medical uses.

He said recognising them as a separate type of organism would put Australia in step with many other countries, including Chile and the United Kingdom.

"There are more fungi than there are plants, and if you were to take the insects out of the animal kingdom, there'd be more fungi than there are animals," Dr Priest said.

"We think that they play an equal role to plants and animals, and so they should be recognised equally."

World.title: Live: Australia's biggest company BHP to report earnings
World.content:
One of Australia's largest super funds Rest has released new research revealing many Aussies are unsure how to navigate the super system and prepare for retirement.

An online survey of 1,432 Rest members aged 18 and above participated in the research in March and April this year.

43% of members say they don't know what steps they need to take to prepare for life after work.

of members say they don't know what steps they need to take to prepare for life after work. 61% of members want greater integration between super funds and Centrelink to help simplify access to the Age Pension.

Rest says this data is significant given 2.7 million Australians aged 65 and over rely on either the full or part Age Pension.

Rest also says 1 in 3 Age Pensioners delay their application by more than a year.

Rest Chief Executive Officer, Vicki Doyle, says there is a growing disconnect in Australia's retirement system.

"Superannuation and the Age Pension are meant to work together, but too often people are left trying to bridge the gap between them," she says. "When people don't know what steps to take as they approach retirement, it's a warning sign that the two biggest parts of Australia's retirement system aren't working together as seamlessly as they should."

From the survey, those aged 46 to 66 were the most likely to describe the retirement system as complex.

"If Australians find the retirement system hardest to navigate at the point they need it most, that's not simply a consumer education issue – it's a system design issue," says Ms Doyle. "Australians need a retirement system that feels like one connected experience, with simpler pathways and better integration between the services they rely on most."

Other significant findings from the research include women and renters feeling particularly unsure and underprepared when thinking about retirement.

Australia's housing market is widening the gap between socioeconomic class, with a 2025 Grattan Institute Report finding home ownership rates among the country's poorest 40% of 45-54 year olds falling from 68% to 54% between 1981 and 2021.

The report found most older working Australians who rent don't have the funds to keep paying rent in retirement, arguing the Commonwealth Rent Assistance program, which supplements the Age Pension for poorer retirees, is too low.

In the previous two budgets, the government lifted the maximum rate of Rent Assistance by 27%. But the Grattan Institute report says despite this, a single retiree who relies solely on income support can afford to rent 4% of one-bedroom homes in Sydney, 13% in Brisbane, and 14% in Melbourne.

Rest Super says higher housing costs can leave renters more reliant on both superannuation and the Age Pension, while older women remain particularly vulnerable to housing insecurity and homelessness.

World.title: Mourners say Jason Arday 'was hunted' by tabloid media before his death
World.content:
Mourners at a London vigil for Jason Arday have accused the British tabloid media of "hunting" the late Cambridge professor, with thousands of people now calling for an inquiry into his death.

Professor Arday died last week following weeks of intense media coverage that questioned the veracity of his extraordinary life story and the provenance of his academic work.

The 41-year-old sociology professor, who made history in 2023 as Cambridge's youngest Black professor, had reportedly told friends his position at the fabled institution was constantly being undermined and university leadership have described the intense press reaction as a "racist feeding frenzy".

At a vigil organised by the campaign group Stand Up To Racism in Trafalgar Square, there was a feeling of immense sadness mixed with visceral anger toward the media.

One attendee told the ABC she believed Dr Arday was "hunted and hunted and hunted until the young man didn't have a choice".

Another mourner stated, "He was a Black man who beat all the odds and succeeded at Cambridge, an institution that we tell our young men to strive for. But he was hounded; it was a witch hunt".

One man described the last few days as "traumatic" as the UK's Black community processed Dr Arday's sudden passing.

Organisers estimated "several thousand" people attended the gathering.

More than 90,000 people have signed a petition seeking an independent inquiry into the media's handling of the academic.

The petition states his death followed "two weeks of relentless harassment".

The press scrutiny focused heavily on Dr Arday's claims he was non-verbal during his childhood, that he had achieved extraordinary athletic feats, and he had signed a lucrative book deal.

Much of the reporting also accused Dr Arday, whose core research revolved around race relations and inequality, of plagiarising his PhD thesis.

More than 90,000 people have signed a petition seeking an independent inquiry into the media's handling of the academic. (Reuters: Chris J Ratcliffe)

Cambridge Chancellor says possible to 'hold to two principles'

Cambridge Chancellor Lord Chris Smith said Dr Arday's treatment had crossed a line.

"I do believe it is possible to hold to two principles at the same time: to believe in the importance of academic integrity, and where criticisms of plagiarism arise about any academic, whoever they are, ensure that they are rigorously investigated," he said.

"And also to refuse to join in a racist feeding frenzy over a particular academic."

Dr Arday resigned from his post on August 5.

In his resignation letter, he emphasised his departure "should not be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

Following his death, a crowdfunding campaign raised more than $300,000 to support funeral costs and his wife and two children.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has declined to state whether the government will formally back a public inquiry described the professor's death as a "tragedy on every level".

World.title: No more discounted sentences for WA criminals due to overcrowded jails
World.content:
Western Australian judges have been told to stop giving criminals reduced sentences because of overcrowding and other alarming issues at the state's prisons.

Earlier this year, WA's prisons watchdog said prisoners were being treated to "cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment" in three jails because the government had allowed the system to become "almost functionally broken".

Some judges had considered those conditions as a mitigating factor in giving shorter sentences to criminals such as Mihael Vrhovsek, who last month had "a chronic shortage of space, significant and inhumane overcrowding" at Hakea Prison taken into account when he was sentenced to 16 years' jail for attempted murder.

But in a decision from WA's Court of Appeal released a week later, three of the state's most senior judges said the practice should stop in most cases.

Judges have been told not take into consideration the conditions at prisons when sentencing criminals. (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

"Some, but not all, sentencing judges do, at least on occasion, take the well-publicised conditions at Hakea into account at sentencing, or at least express some sympathy for offenders who have been enduring ongoing lock down conditions," the trio wrote.

" To the contrary, the weight of opinion is that such conditions cannot properly be taken into account. "

But the judges stressed their decision did not mean that the Supreme Court was endorsing current prison conditions.

"None of this is to suggest that this court does not share the legitimate concern expressed by others as to the conditions in which prisoners are housed in facilities which are overstretched and under-resourced," the judges wrote.

Decision 'concerning'

The court's decision does not mean prior sentences were incorrect, University of Western Australia law school lecturer Jamie Walvisch said.

"This is more about clarifying the situation moving forwards … there's definitely been a bit of a grey area until now," he said.

UWA law school lecturer Jamie Walvisch says prior sentences factoring in prison conditions were not wrong. (ABC News: Jon Kerr)

He said individual prisoners could still receive a discounted sentence if that overcrowding would have a more detrimental effect on them because of factors like their age, disability or mental ill-health.

Prisoners receiving compensation for overcrowding in WA prisons Prisoners are receiving financial compensation for sleeping on the floor due to overcrowding across Western Australian jails, the ABC can reveal.

But the effect of the appalling conditions at the prisons went far beyond a few individuals, he added.

"If a prisoner has no access to educational services, to rehabilitative programs, to fresh air and [is] living in conditions where they are being subject to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, then they are unlikely to be rehabilitated," he said.

"If we want to really address the problem of crime then we should be putting more money into providing services and programs to assist prisoners rather than making their conditions intolerable."

Casuarina Prison is one of the facilities listed in the damning prisons watchdog report. (ABC News: James Carmody)

'No passing the buck'

Shadow Attorney-General Nick Goiran said the Court of Appeal had now "added its voice to the chorus of alarm about the state of Western Australia's prisons".

Damning report on state of WA prisons WA prisoners are being subjected to "cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment" because the state government has allowed prisons to become "almost fundamentally broken", according to the Inspector of Custodial Services.

He added there could be "no passing of the buck" given Attorney-General Tony Buti recently took on the corrective services portfolio.

"After nearly a decade of inaction, the time has surely come for the Cook Labor government to ensure our prisons are capable of rehabilitating offenders and protecting the community when those offenders are eventually released," he said.

Dr Buti said one of his first actions after taking on the portfolio was to seek an "urgent briefing" on overcrowding.

Tony Buti says the state government is working to improve prison conditions. (ABC News: James Carmody )

"There are challenges facing the state's corrective services system. But Western Australia is not unique in regard to rising prisoner numbers, increasingly complex offender cohorts, and workforce demands," he said in a statement.

The minister said "community safety" was the government's first priority, and that this year's budget included more than $300 million in new money for justice and corrective services.

"We are investing in infrastructure that will bring more beds online and provide opportunity for prisoners to engage in meaningful activities while serving their sentence," he said.

World.title: Mangione's NYC trial postponed indefinitely amid double jeopardy fight
World.content:
Luigi Mangione's New York murder trial in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, which was slated to begin in weeks, has been postponed indefinitely as his lawyers seek to have the case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.

It comes following Mangione's guilty plea last week to federal charges.

Judge Gregory Carro issued an order on Monday, local time, cancelling the trial and giving the Manhattan District Attorney's Office, which is prosecuting the state case, until October 9 to respond to the defence's double jeopardy claims.

A hearing will be held on December 10, Judge Carro said, about a week before Mangione is scheduled to be sentenced in the federal case.

Luigi Mangione has pleaded guilty to trailing the UnitedHealth Group's CEO and gunning him down outside a Manhattan hotel in 2024. (Reuters: Steven Hirsch/Pool)

Mangione, 28, pleaded guilty on Friday in Manhattan federal court to a pair of stalking charges and admitted trailing Mr Thompson to UnitedHealth Group's investor conference and shooting him outside a Manhattan hotel in 2024.

Federal prosecutors said they would seek life in prison when Mangione is sentenced in December, although federal sentencing guidelines call for a term of 24 to 30 years.

"On the morning of December 4, 2024, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan, and he died," Mangione said.

Immediately after his plea, Mangione's lawyers sought to have the state case thrown out on double jeopardy and due process grounds.

They described him as a "pawn in parallel prosecutions" and accused state and federal prosecutors of "trying to punish him twice for the exact conduct".

Loved ones lay bare the makings of alleged gunman Luigi Mangione The family and friends of alleged UnitedHealthcare CEO gunman Luigi Mangione unravel how he could have gone from valedictorian to an accused killer.

Mangione has pleaded not guilty in the state case, which also carries the possibility of a life sentence.

Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg's office said in a statement it would fight efforts to end the state case, in part because Mangione's federal sentence is not yet known.

Compared with federal law and that of other states, New York has uncommonly strong protections for defendants facing multiple prosecutions.

A state prosecution can be barred if a federal case involving the same course of conduct or criminal transaction ends in a guilty plea or if a jury is sworn.

Judge Carro will decide whether that applies to Mangione.

Judge Carro's ruling will also be subject to appeal.

Luigi Mangione travelled across state lines by bus to stalk Brian Thompson and stayed at a hostel while planning the attack. (Reuters: Jane Rosenberg)

Mangione pleaded guilty to federal charges that accused him of travelling across state lines by bus to stalk and kill Mr Thompson and staying at a hostel that serves out-of-state customers while planning and carrying out the attack.

"The full range of conduct that comprises the stalking offence is coterminous with the conduct committed as part of the murder offence," Mangione's lawyers wrote in their double jeopardy filing.

That he travelled from out of state "to be at the crime scene at the time of the shooting does nothing to eliminate the stalking of Mr Thompson from the acts constituting his murder", Mangione's lawyers wrote.

"They are all part of the same criminal incident or criminal transaction."

Mr Bragg's office contends that the state charges, including murder and firearms offences, involve different legal elements and criminal conduct.

In a letter last month, Assistant District Attorney Joel Seidemann objected to the possibility of a federal guilty plea wiping out the state case.

Any guilty plea, Mr Seidemann wrote, "must account for the seriousness of defendant's offences" and for the state's interests in prosecuting Mangione, "including the sanctity of life principle that underpins the state homicide charges".

AP

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor to launch ‘opt-out’ register for gambling ads; Trump threatens to bomb Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires
World.content:
Chalmers is continuing on the breakfast news circuit, and has been asked about the changes the government would consider making to betting inducements in its package of gambling reforms.

Speaking to ABC’s News Breakfast this morning, the treasurer said:

World.title: The Test team’s five biggest problems: Is Lyon an automatic selection?
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket The Test team’s five biggest problems: Is Lyon an automatic selection? Daniel Brettig Updated August 18, 2026 — 7:51am ,first published 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Top order batting – Pat Cummins asked his batting order to get through a tricky first couple of hours on a fresh pitch in Darwin and they were completely unable to find a way to do so against a diligent but far from fearsome Bangladesh attack. Jake Weatherald’s perpetual motion at the crease speaks of technical tweaks but also nerves, and it is tough to see him keeping his place in Mackay. Marnus Labuschagne has already been dropped and recalled once in the past year, but is still struggling to find his best. Then there’s Travis Head and the question of his best position. Former opener Matthew Hayden was one seasoned voice to call for Matt Renshaw and Sam Konstas at the top, with Head moving to three. Ebadot Hossain of Bangladesh celebrates after taking the wicket of Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Tellingly, Cummins spoke not of a one-off problem but of a trend, meaning that the team’s batting difficulties will be the chief topic of internal conversation this week. He was also open about the selectors’ ability to make change: “Every Aussie Test we do you can kind of pick whatever, it’s not a World Cup squad. You’ve got a lot of available guys who are ready to go.” As Alyssa Healy put it on Fox Cricket: “It’s almost like they’ve underestimated themselves a little bit, the Bangladeshis. I mean, the whole of Australia probably did as well, but it’s almost like their humble approach has worked for them. We’ve got carried away with how big this summer is, but this is a wake-up call for Australia. Probably what they needed as well, after breezing through last summer.”



Nathan Lyon – In his first game back from hamstring surgery, 38-year-old Lyon was ineffective, certainly relative to the Bangladesh spinners, and also dropped a vital catch. There is no doubt Australia will need Lyon’s skills in India next year, but questions must be asked about whether he is an automatic selection, either ahead of Scott Boland or also the younger left-arm spinner Matt Kuhnemann. Meanwhile, Lyon needs to regain his ability to deceive batsmen in the air – Bangladesh had few problems reading his length here, despite a helpful breeze at times. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Cummins flags batting changes after Australia’s bubble burst by Bangladesh Cummins said of Boland: “With Scotty, we all know how good he is, so we’ll turn up in Mackay, have a look at the pitch and work out your best bowling group. But with someone like Scotty in the squad you’re always trying to find a way to fit him in, he’s that good.” Domestic pitches – Something an excellent Darwin surface exposed was how Bangladesh’s batters were better equipped to keep out good balls and bat time, a theme that runs well down the ranks into the Sheffield Shield. Partly this is because of a preponderance of grassy result pitches that make life difficult for batters and a little too easy for seamers.



A topic of conversation at a recent Cricket Australia summit in Brisbane, it’s an issue that Head has highlighted the difficulty of: “You can sit outside and say we want a great balance between bat and ball, but if you ask the states and the boards and who runs the show, they’ll say we want to win Shields, so I don’t think they’d care less on what it looks like, they want performance and they want to win.” Talent pipeline – A major reason Australia are fielding their oldest ever Test team is a high level of selection scepticism about the younger talent coming through, something backed up by modest Shield aggregates in recent summers. Australian coach Andrew McDonald and Josh Hazlewood. Getty Images Based on those figures, there is no-one better available, but it will be up to the selectors to make some calculated gambles that go beyond pure statistics. Bangladesh provided a good reminder of that by how 25-year-old Tanzid Hasan (first-class batting average 39) and 26-year-old Hasan Mahmud (bowling average 28) seized their opportunities. Succession plan – Australia’s huge allotment of Tests over the next 12 months leaves open the question of whether the current regime will change out of exhaustion as much as anything else next year. But the conversations need to start now, and in some cases they already have.



Head coach Andrew McDonald’s deal expires at the end of 2027, while Cummins’ captaincy tenure is also of uncertain duration. It may be easier to replace McDonald with one of Ryan Harris, Adam Voges or Tim Paine, but it is also a concern that Cummins’ stand-in remains the 37-year-old Steve Smith, whose career has operated on a series by series basis for several years. World.title: ‘The money will come’: Why Pritchard brothers turned down PNG riches to stay in rugby
World.content:
Exclusive SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘The money will come’: Why Pritchard brothers turned down PNG riches to stay in rugby Jonathan Drennan August 18, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before making the biggest decision of their young professional careers, Treyvon and Kadin Pritchard thought back to two important lessons taught to them by their parents, Daniel and Brenda: never leave a job half done, and always show loyalty to those who backed you from the start. The brothers ultimately turned down the lucrative offer tabled by the PNG Chiefs to join the NRL expansion franchise for its inaugural season in 2028, opting instead to remain at their respective rugby clubs, with Treyvon signing an extension with the Reds until 2029 and Kadin remaining at the Brumbies until 2030. Both brothers also have the opportunity to play sevens in the 2028 Olympics. Treyvon (L) and Kadin Pritchard are staying in Australian rugby. Rugby Australia “I think from a young age mum and dad have always instilled in us the value of finishing what you’ve started and never doing a half job,” Treyvon told this masthead. “Our parents taught us to finish what we’ve started. Loyalty does come into play, too. It’s a big part of our everyday lives and something that our parents have made us follow, and it’s led into our everyday life.



“Also, coming through from being a 15-year-old in the Reds environment to moving up and training with the older boys while I was still in school with a couple of my mates. “We all have come through at the same time and we have those connections, and I think a big thing with footy is being able to trust your teammates. If you already have something in place, there’s no real reason to kind of change that and switch it up. Treyvon is one of the most exciting talents in Australian rugby. World Rugby “So I think the friendships and the connections that I already have are also a big part of my reasoning to stay in Australian rugby.” The brothers spoke highly of their dealings with the Chiefs, but ultimately turned down the lucrative offer because they felt they have unfinished business in rugby together – and believe the money will follow them eventually.



“Obviously, it was exciting [to get the PNG offer] and yeah, we did meet with them, and I think that was probably both our first real kind interest from league. So we tested the waters and we were trying to see what it was all about,” Treyvon said. “But I think Rugby Australia had a lot to offer as well. Like I said before, loyalty played a big part in where we are now and that helped us to a decision on where we wanted to be for the next couple of years... “The money is going to come, it’s probably not the biggest worry at the moment. We need to focus on establishing ourselves in our respective teams.” Kadin said that beyond immediate financial rewards, rugby will offer the brothers a chance to travel the world while playing the game they love. “I love rugby union and the possibilities that it can bring with the worldwide game were a big thing for me to stay here,” Kadin said.



“To travel around the world, playing international teams – and even if it’s club level, you can go over somewhere like France. The possibilities of doing that sort of thing, you don’t get that in other sports.” The Ella brothers brought an almost telepathic understanding to the Wallabies back line in the 1980s and the Pritchards believe they can eventually replicate that synergy as a centre partnership for the Australian Test team. Kadin Pritchard dreams of forming a centre partnership with Treyvon at Test level for the Wallabies . Getty Images “It’s definitely a dream of ours to link up at some point,” Kadin said. “We’ve been separated for a reason: to build ourselves up in our own teams and build the groups around us. “By the time we get to the Wallabies, we’ll be set to go, because we’ve got that brother intuition ... we want to play together in the centres, with Trayvon at inside centre.



“It’s definitely been a thought in my mind becoming that 12 and 13, and you probably don’t see it too often having brothers in the centres with that connection. We’re just almost interlinked and we know how each other plays from doing it so often in the backyard.” Having spent endless hours playing together as kids, the two brothers came up against each other for the first time last season, when the Reds faced the Brumbies in Super Rugby. But Treyvon says it is when playing together on the same side that their close relationship brings an extra edge. “We probably don’t have to speak as much as other players would; we can communicate with our body language and trust is a big factor in the connection that we have over other players,” Treyvon said. At 22 years old, Kadin has always felt protective of Treyvon, who is three years younger than him. Treyvon affectionately calls Kadin the family’s “test dummy”, the older brother who had to forge the way into professional rugby before passing on the lessons learned along the way. Though separated by distance, the brothers still speak regularly and operate as a unit when it comes to making decisions on their rugby future.



The brothers have been brought up to support one another, wary that there will always be others outside the family who want to tear one or another of them down. “We know what each other can do and why should we hate on our family when you’ve got haters outside already,” Kadin said. “The tightness of our family, it’s just been brought through by our dad. Treyvon Pritchard suffered serious injuries in this hip drop tackle against Wales at the Junior World Championship, but is recovering well after surgery. Stan Sport “We’re our own biggest supporters, we’ve got to support each other and build each other up so there’s no hate coming from within, and we have a support group here. “There’s no way I’m going to hate on what my bro’s doing. I’m just going to hype him up to be the best player in the world. What’s the point of trying to pull him down when everybody else is trying to do that?”



Both brothers are currently recovering from injuries. Kadin is nursing a hamstring strain but hopes to return to play for the Brumbies in the Super Rugby AUS competition, while Treyvon is recovering from an operation after breaking his right leg ain a hip drop tackle while representing Australia Under 20s. Treyvon’s current recovery timeline is between 12 and 18 weeks. Related Article Australian rugby ‘Run us off our feet’: Wallabies’ surprising ploy to prepare for Japanese heat Both brothers are focused on establishing their positions with their respective Super Rugby clubs ahead of a new season, but Treyvon is aware there will always be future possibilities, whether in rugby or the NRL. “We’re definitely not closed off to playing overseas, and I think once we make a decision on that, I think we would probably look to play together, I don’t see why we wouldn’t,” Treyvon said. “I think living in a different country is hard enough, so I think being with the older bro would be awesome. “I’m [also] not closed off to the NRL. Obviously all the noise that’s been happening recently probably sparked a bit of interest for everyone, but it’s definitely an option down the track. I’m with the Reds for three years and with Aussie rugby for three years, so whatever happens after that happen.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil prices climb; BHP, CSL results ahead
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil prices climb; BHP, CSL results ahead Stan Choe Updated August 18, 2026 — 6:24am ,first published 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks edged further from their record heights on Monday after rising oil prices cranked up the pressure on inflation and financial markets. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent but remains near its all-time high set Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 272 points, or 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.3 per cent. Wall Street opened the week with more losses. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 6.04am AEST pointing to a fall of 40 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US71.03¢. Reporting season continues with BHP and CSL results slated to be released today. Wall Street’s losses solidified in the afternoon when oil prices accelerated upward. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 2.7 per cent to $US90.87.



Related Article Exclusive

James Packer James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares It’s been careening back and forth because of uncertainty about what the war with Iran will do to the global flow of crude. Last month alone, Brent zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. Monday’s rally for oil prices sent Treasury yields in the bond market higher, which in turn raised the pressure on the economy and prices for all kinds of investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 4.72 per cent from 4.68 per cent late Friday. It has shot up from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran, largely because higher oil prices are worsening inflation and upping the probability that the Federal Reserve will have to hike interest rates. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy. The average long-term US mortgage rate has already jumped near its highest level in a year because of the rise in the 10-year Treasury yield, though reports last week said that inflation in July was not as bad as earlier in the summer.



Usually around this time of year, anticipation is building on Wall Street to hear from the head of the Federal Reserve about where it may take interest rates. But the Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, may give little insight at this year’s economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of this month, according to Thierry Wizman, a strategist at Macquarie Group Warsh has been adamant about giving Wall Street less guidance about the Fed’s plans for interest rates. Wall Street has run to records despite high inflation in large part because profits are booming for U.S. companies. Those in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver growth of roughly 50 per cent for earnings per share in the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That’s much better than analysts expected and would be the best since five years ago, when the economy was erupting out of the chasm created by the COVID pandemic. Nearly all the companies in the S&P 500 have turned in their profit reports for the spring. Still to come are big retailers, including reports this week from Home Depot, Target and Walmart.



Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Trump makes America Inc’s grip on the world even tighter They’re facing pressure. Their customers’ incomes may be turning iffier after U.S. employers surprisingly cut more jobs last month than they added. At the same time, their customers are continuing to see bills rise quickly as inflation remains much higher than anyone would like. A report last week said that shoppers surprisingly spent less at U.S. retailers last month than in June, and CEOs for retailers could give color this week on what they’re seeing. On Wall Street, trading was relatively quiet Monday. L3Harris Technologies fell 4.6 per cent after the defense company said Christopher Kubasik stepped down as its CEO and chairman following “certain conduct by Kubasik that was not consistent with the values of the Company.” It gave few details but said the conduct was not related to its financial reporting, controls, customer relationships or operational performance.



Alphabet dipped 0.5 per cent even though Berkshire Hathaway said it increased its investment in Google’s parent company, along with several homebuilders. Berkshire built a reputation for buying stocks at affordable prices under its former CEO, famed investor Warren Buffett. Constellation Brands fell 6.2 per cent after Berkshire said it sold all its holdings in the seller of Modelo beer and Robert Mondavi wine. All told, the S&P 500 fell 40.70 points to 7,745.06. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 272.63 to 53,459.78, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 84.25 to 26,644.91. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped in Europe following a stronger finish in Asia. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7 per cent after a report said Japan’s economy grew at a slower pace in the April-June quarter than economists expected. Indexes jumped 1.3 per cent in Hong Kong and 1.4 per cent in Shanghai for some of the world’s biggest moves.

World.title: More than 2.6 million Australians will be living with cancer diagnosis by 2050, say scientists
World.content:
Exclusive NationalHealthcare More than 2.6 million Australians will be living with cancer diagnosis by 2050, say scientists Melissa Cunningham August 18, 2026 — 5:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 2.6 million Australians are forecast to be living with a cancer diagnosis by 2050 – an increase of 1 million people over the next 25 years. For the first time, researchers have used scientific modelling to estimate the prevalence of cancer in Australia in the future, including those in active treatment and people who have survived the disease, but require ongoing care. Naveena Nekkalapudi, pictured with her dog, Laika, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2014. She is now cancer-free, but lives with ongoing nerve pain. Wayne Taylor The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific medical journal, predicted breast cancer would be the nation’s most prevalent cancer in 2050, followed by prostate, melanoma, colorectal and kidney cancer. Almost 1.7 million Australians have cancer or are in the post-treatment phase of the disease, but by 2050, researchers have predicted the total number of people living with cancer will rise by 57 per cent to more than 2.6 million.



Currently, the nation’s population is about 28 million, but by 2050, the Australian Bureau of Statistics estimates it could grow to between 32 and 38 million, depending on fertility rates, migration and life expectancy. Related Article Cancer Revealed: The radical overhaul of cancer screening to detect most at risk Population growth, a rise in ageing Australians and a soaring incidence of certain cancer types are expected to prompt a surge in people being diagnosed. Roughly 44 per cent of the 2.6 million Australians forecast to be living with cancer by 2050 are expected to have an incurable cancer that will require ongoing treatment. “Our projections suggest that in 2050, while more than half of people with a past cancer diagnosis will be potentially cured (1.47 million), about 1.15 million people will be living with cancer (cancers not yet cured) and requiring active treatment or ongoing care,” the researchers wrote.



But in hopeful news, researchers predicted that in the future, cancer survival rates would improve thanks to earlier detection and advancements in treatments such as pioneering immunotherapy. They predicted this would lead to a record rise in people living longer with the disease or being declared “cancer-free” following treatment. Professor Michael Jefford, a co-senior author of the research, and the director of the Australian Cancer Survivorship Centre at Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, said national survival rates had improved remarkably in the past 20 years. “The five-year survival rate for all cancers in Australia is over 70 per cent, which is the highest it’s ever been,” the medical oncologist said. “People are having cancer detected at an early stage and at a stage where it can be cured.”



Jefford said while the number of cases diagnosed would continue to climb, the research highlighted a “huge” increase in cancer survivors, many of whom would have other illnesses or ongoing health issues as a result of the disease or their age. Professor Michael Jefford says national survival rates have improved remarkably in the past 20 years. Simon Schluter Melbourne woman Naveena Nekkalapudi was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2014 at age 39. Nekkalapudi is now cancer-free and counts herself lucky. But bouts of intensive chemotherapy permanently damaged her nerves, leading to a condition known as peripheral neuropathy. “In my case, it’s ongoing chronic pain, it’s pins and needles, it’s shooting and burning pain,” she said. “I call it the gremlins jabbing a pin into my big toe at night … you can’t do anything about it.”



For more than eight years, Nekkalapudi, 51, needed a pain management specialist, and she continued to take medication to control her symptoms. Related Article Good Weekend First we read DNA. Then we edited. Now we’re learning to write Jefford warned an overhaul of Australia’s healthcare system was urgently needed to meet the mounting demand. He said managing the large numbers of people surviving or living with the disease would require new models of care. This could include care led by general practitioners or nurses, and remote monitoring of lower-risk patients to ease pressure on hospitals and cancer centres. “We know that survivors have significant unmet needs and that existing models of care do not adequately manage these,” Jefford said.



“Survivorship care should focus not just on surveillance for possible recurrence and second cancers but should also focus on the management of physical and psychosocial issues, health promotion and disease prevention, and management of chronic health conditions.” Nekkalapudi, who is a carer for her mum who has also survived breast cancer, called for a focus on early prevention of the disease. She also wanted patients to be provided support “before, during and after” treatment to help them prevent or manage any long-term toxicity complications, which might arise as a result of their treatment. The study was a collaboration between Melbourne’s Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, the University of Sydney, the Daffodil Centre and the Cancer Council NSW. The study’s lead author, University of Sydney’s Associate Professor Qingwei Luo, said the findings demonstrated that cancer was increasingly becoming a long-term, chronic condition rather than a short-term illness.



However, the epidemiologist at the Daffodil Centre, a partnership between Cancer Council NSW and the University of Sydney, warned the largest increase in cancer prevalence was predicted to occur among Australians aged 80 and over, a demographic projected to more than double from 481,000 in 2025 to more than 1 million by 2050. An image of changes in cells indicative of prostate cancer. AP “Many of these [people] will have complex needs, multiple chronic conditions, and long-term treatment effects,” Luo said. Breast cancer is projected to be Australia’s most prevalent cancer in 2050, with more than 485,000 cases up from 298,109 in 2025. This is predicted to be followed by prostate cancer, which researchers estimate will increase from 309,663 cases to 468,991 in the next 25 years. Meanwhile, melanoma cases are forecast to reach 331,909 and colorectal cancer cases are forecast to rise to 237,053. The number of people being given a kidney cancer diagnosis is also set to increase by 121 per cent, soaring from 48,908 last year to 108,101 cases in 2050.



The increase in diagnoses is due to more people living beyond the age of 60, and more people living longer with the disease due to targeted therapies and early detection. Editor's pick Exclusive

Investigation The corrupt relatives behind one of Australia’s richest people These five conditions would account for more than 62 per cent of all Australians living with or beyond a cancer diagnosis by mid-century, the researchers said. World.title: This is, hands down, the most confronting thing I’ve seen on screen all year
World.content:
Alex Gibney is no stranger to challenging material. But his film about the stabbing of Salman Rushdie takes some topping.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s Melbourne International Film Festival has kicked off. Here we take a closer look at some of what’s on offer. See all stories .

As Salman Rushdie lay in hospital after being repeatedly stabbed on stage in August 2022, his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths started filming. Asking if he was OK with that, he told her yes. “We need to document this.” Now, Alex Gibney has turned that raw, unflinching and often hard-to-watch footage into Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie, one of the most confronting, but ultimately hopeful, movies you’ll ever see. “On this film, I acted mostly as an editor,” says the prolific documentarian who won an Oscar (with Australian producer Eva Orner) for Taxi to the Dark Side in 2007 and has five Emmy wins to his name. “My agent told me Salman and Eliza were interested in talking to me, and I learned they had this footage that Eliza took, starting on day five of his recovery and going right up to when they returned to the scene of the crime. And the first question I asked them was, ‘Why don’t you do it? No one knows more about what happened than you do’. And they said, ‘Well, that’s the problem. We feel too close to it. We want somebody else to come in and see if they can figure out a way to reckon with it.’” Gibney pitched an approach informed by The Singing Detective, the 1986 BBC drama series written by Dennis Potter, in which Michael Gambon played a bed-bound writer in hospital whose medication produces a blurring of his imaginative world and his memories. Despite its complex (and much-praised) structure, the show could be boiled down, says Gibney, to a pretty simple idea: a guy who is sick gets better, but along the way he reimagines his life through hallucinations and his detective fiction.



Rushdie, who had not yet decided to write his own account of the incident (his book Knife: Meditation on an Attempted Murder was released in August 2024), liked the idea, and the film Gibney has made – with Griffiths credited as executive producer and principal cinematographer – serves both as an account of the attack and its aftermath and as a meditation on Rushdie’s life more broadly. Knife opens with a recreation of the attack, with Rushdie asking in voiceover, “Why didn’t I fight back?” It’s a shocking way to start, but it’s nothing compared to what follows. Staff and audience members come to Rushdie’s aid at the Chautauqua Institution on August 12, 2022. AP The Booker Prize winner was in a chair on the stage of the Chautauqua Institution in New York State, about to be interviewed, when a man armed with a knife rushed up the steps and lunged at him. The attacker, Hadi Matar, stabbed the novelist 15 times, landing blows in his neck, stomach, chest and thigh. One of them struck Rushdie, who was 76 at the time, in his right eye (he has lost all sight in it). Matar had been inspired by the fatwa issued by Iran in 1989 in response to Rushdie’s novel The Satanic Verses, which Ayatollah Khomeini and his fellow clerics had deemed blasphemous. (Iran’s position on the fatwa has since become somewhat ambiguous, but it has never officially been rescinded. Last month a trial on terrorism charges against Matar – who has already been convicted of attempted murder – began in Buffalo, New York.) The film also includes real footage of the attack, which was only released during Matar’s first trial in February 2025. It’s horrendous in its brutality, and Gibney admits he wasn’t sure that he should even include it. “I mean, for a documentarian, it would be very hard not to show the actual crime, but I did ponder that maybe we shouldn’t,” he says. What got him over the line was the footage Griffiths had shot of her and Rushdie returning to Chautauqua, “and within that context it seemed to make sense to show it”.



The most challenging scenes in the film, though, are probably the shots of Rushdie’s horribly disfigured eyeball, bulging from its socket, occluded, pointing wildly out of focus. “Trust me,” says Gibney, “in a theatre you can hear the whole audience go ‘aagh’. It’s very difficult to watch.” There was never any chance of not including that footage, though. “Both of them [Rushdie and Griffiths] felt very strongly that they wanted to show this is what terrorism looks like.” For all that Griffiths’ footage was the rock on which the film is built, Gibney knew he had to go beyond it to tell the story he had in mind. “Too much of that, and it’s only about his physical recovery, rather than a deeper kind of mental recovery,” he says. “And once you enter the mind, it’s a chaotic and unpredictable place, and you have to sort of go with the flow.” Rushdie’s wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths, began filming from five days after the attack. They had been married less than a year when it happened. Getty In archival footage, interviews from across the decades and in his own scripted narration, Rushdie reflects on being an outsider in his own family in Mumbai, of feeling the lash of racism at the English boarding school (Rugby) to which he was sent by his father when he was 14, of the cold shoulder some in the literary establishment turned on him when Iran called for his murder, with the offer of a massive bounty (starting at $1 million, it eventually rose to $6 million). There’s a sense overall of a man wounded many times in his life, and of his attempt to stitch himself back together in spite of it all. Whatever you might think of Rushdie, it’s impossible not to be moved by his resilience, his unflinching commitment to free speech, and his refusal of hatred.

World.title: Trump threatens to bomb ally Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Trump threatens to bomb ally Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires Michael Koziol August 18, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: US President Donald Trump threatened to bomb US ally Oman if it “gets in the way” of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while casting doubt on the possibility of reaching a new deal with Iran after their 60-day interim agreement expired. Next week will mark six months since the US and Israel launched a joint attack on the Islamic Republic. Although the fighting has subsided, the US continues to impose a naval blockade against Iran, and a permanent deal to end the conflict and restore free shipping remains elusive. Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Monday. He said Iran was not willing to make the kind of deal he thought acceptable. AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta In an interview with Fox News, Trump reportedly confirmed the existence of back-channel communications between the US and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the hardline militants responsible for shooting drones and missiles at ships in the strait. Iran and Oman – an American partner on the Arabian Peninsula, which sits across the Gulf of Oman from Iran – have been engaged in talks about management of the crucial waterway, as stipulated by the Memorandum of Understanding signed by the US and Iran in June. That agreement expired on Monday (Washington time).



At a news conference, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said talks with Oman continued. The process was taking longer, he said, as multiple countries were trying to influence the outcome. The parties have suggested an agreement was close for nearly two weeks. Trump told Fox News on Monday: “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them.” Later, in the Oval Office, he struck a different tone: “I don’t think [Oman] behave very well, but we handle them.” Iranian children swim in the Strait of Hormuz as cargo ships are anchored in the distance. Getty Images It is not the first time Trump has made such a threat, as Oman has previously countenanced the idea of setting up a tolling system in the strait with Iran. He insisted the November midterm elections were not a factor in his thinking, despite many Iran experts arguing that Tehran was trying to run down the clock on Trump’s patience and political capital. Brent crude oil was trading at above $US90 a barrel on Monday.



Trump also repeated his desire to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, having teased the idea at a rally in Long Island, New York, last week. But he offered no explanation as to how that would work, nor what – if anything – it would entail. “We control it with the blockade. I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” Trump told reporters. “[Iran] can be a nuisance, they can put a mine in the water. But the blockade has been very effective.” Trump in the Oval Office on Monday, where he met with lifeguard Ryder Williams, left. AP The president also cast doubt on whether an acceptable deal with Iran to end the war and reopen the strait was possible. He implied that Iran was in a parlous state, which may lead it to reconsider its position at a later date. “They want to make a deal, but they’re not going to make the kind of deal that I feel is necessary,” he said. “Iran is in big trouble. They have 300 per cent inflation. The country is a mess and their military is totally defeated.”



Meanwhile, the US is relocating the USS George Washington aircraft carrier from the Asia-Pacific to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, which is heading home amid growing concerns about living conditions on-board after a record-breaking deployment. That decision means there are no American aircraft carriers left in the Pacific. Addressing the apparent Middle East stalemate on Monday, Iran analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at the Israel-based Institute for National Security Studies, said the regime would not capitulate. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian with the memorandum of understanding signed with US in June. Iranian Presidency Office via AP “In the choice between submission and escalation, Iran will choose escalation,” he wrote on X. “One can debate its scope, timing, and the tools it will employ, but the expectation that American pressure will bring Tehran to raise the white flag is incompatible with the way the Iranian regime perceives itself and its survival.” Last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent flagged unprecedented sanctions against Iran in an attempt to apply even more economic pressure on the weakened regime. He has not yet announced further measures.



Related Article Updated

Trump diplomacy Trump praises North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, slashes military drills with Seoul Aaron David Miller, a Middle East analyst who was formerly a long-time State Department negotiator, said it could include secondary sanctions that cut off any country or bank doing business with Iran from the US financial system, or directly targeting Chinese purchases of Iranian oil. “That’s a severe sanction,” he said. “It would involve everybody, including Australia.” But Miller said he did not believe it would make much difference. “I don’t think any of these things will in a reasonable period of time change Iran’s calculation on the core issues.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The Test team’s five biggest problems: Is Lyon an automatic selection?
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket The Test team’s five biggest problems: Is Lyon an automatic selection? Daniel Brettig Updated August 18, 2026 — 7:51am ,first published 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Top order batting – Pat Cummins asked his batting order to get through a tricky first couple of hours on a fresh pitch in Darwin and they were completely unable to find a way to do so against a diligent but far from fearsome Bangladesh attack. Jake Weatherald’s perpetual motion at the crease speaks of technical tweaks but also nerves, and it is tough to see him keeping his place in Mackay. Marnus Labuschagne has already been dropped and recalled once in the past year, but is still struggling to find his best. Then there’s Travis Head and the question of his best position. Former opener Matthew Hayden was one seasoned voice to call for Matt Renshaw and Sam Konstas at the top, with Head moving to three. Ebadot Hossain of Bangladesh celebrates after taking the wicket of Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Tellingly, Cummins spoke not of a one-off problem but of a trend, meaning that the team’s batting difficulties will be the chief topic of internal conversation this week. He was also open about the selectors’ ability to make change: “Every Aussie Test we do you can kind of pick whatever, it’s not a World Cup squad. You’ve got a lot of available guys who are ready to go.” As Alyssa Healy put it on Fox Cricket: “It’s almost like they’ve underestimated themselves a little bit, the Bangladeshis. I mean, the whole of Australia probably did as well, but it’s almost like their humble approach has worked for them. We’ve got carried away with how big this summer is, but this is a wake-up call for Australia. Probably what they needed as well, after breezing through last summer.”



Nathan Lyon – In his first game back from hamstring surgery, 38-year-old Lyon was ineffective, certainly relative to the Bangladesh spinners, and also dropped a vital catch. There is no doubt Australia will need Lyon’s skills in India next year, but questions must be asked about whether he is an automatic selection, either ahead of Scott Boland or also the younger left-arm spinner Matt Kuhnemann. Meanwhile, Lyon needs to regain his ability to deceive batsmen in the air – Bangladesh had few problems reading his length here, despite a helpful breeze at times. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Cummins flags batting changes after Australia’s bubble burst by Bangladesh Cummins said of Boland: “With Scotty, we all know how good he is, so we’ll turn up in Mackay, have a look at the pitch and work out your best bowling group. But with someone like Scotty in the squad you’re always trying to find a way to fit him in, he’s that good.” Domestic pitches – Something an excellent Darwin surface exposed was how Bangladesh’s batters were better equipped to keep out good balls and bat time, a theme that runs well down the ranks into the Sheffield Shield. Partly this is because of a preponderance of grassy result pitches that make life difficult for batters and a little too easy for seamers.



A topic of conversation at a recent Cricket Australia summit in Brisbane, it’s an issue that Head has highlighted the difficulty of: “You can sit outside and say we want a great balance between bat and ball, but if you ask the states and the boards and who runs the show, they’ll say we want to win Shields, so I don’t think they’d care less on what it looks like, they want performance and they want to win.” Talent pipeline – A major reason Australia are fielding their oldest ever Test team is a high level of selection scepticism about the younger talent coming through, something backed up by modest Shield aggregates in recent summers. Australian coach Andrew McDonald and Josh Hazlewood. Getty Images Based on those figures, there is no-one better available, but it will be up to the selectors to make some calculated gambles that go beyond pure statistics. Bangladesh provided a good reminder of that by how 25-year-old Tanzid Hasan (first-class batting average 39) and 26-year-old Hasan Mahmud (bowling average 28) seized their opportunities. Succession plan – Australia’s huge allotment of Tests over the next 12 months leaves open the question of whether the current regime will change out of exhaustion as much as anything else next year. But the conversations need to start now, and in some cases they already have.



Head coach Andrew McDonald’s deal expires at the end of 2027, while Cummins’ captaincy tenure is also of uncertain duration. It may be easier to replace McDonald with one of Ryan Harris, Adam Voges or Tim Paine, but it is also a concern that Cummins’ stand-in remains the 37-year-old Steve Smith, whose career has operated on a series by series basis for several years. World.content:

No foul play is suspected in the death of American actor Hayden Panettiere, police said, as emergency dispatch audio published by several US outlets indicated the star was in cardiac arrest following a suspected overdose.

World.title: ‘The money will come’: Why Pritchard brothers turned down PNG riches to stay in rugby
World.content:
Exclusive SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘The money will come’: Why Pritchard brothers turned down PNG riches to stay in rugby Jonathan Drennan August 18, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Before making the biggest decision of their young professional careers, Treyvon and Kadin Pritchard thought back to two important lessons taught to them by their parents, Daniel and Brenda: never leave a job half done, and always show loyalty to those who backed you from the start. The brothers ultimately turned down the lucrative offer tabled by the PNG Chiefs to join the NRL expansion franchise for its inaugural season in 2028, opting instead to remain at their respective rugby clubs, with Treyvon signing an extension with the Reds until 2029 and Kadin remaining at the Brumbies until 2030. Both brothers also have the opportunity to play sevens in the 2028 Olympics. Treyvon (L) and Kadin Pritchard are staying in Australian rugby. Rugby Australia “I think from a young age mum and dad have always instilled in us the value of finishing what you’ve started and never doing a half job,” Treyvon told this masthead. “Our parents taught us to finish what we’ve started. Loyalty does come into play, too. It’s a big part of our everyday lives and something that our parents have made us follow, and it’s led into our everyday life.



“Also, coming through from being a 15-year-old in the Reds environment to moving up and training with the older boys while I was still in school with a couple of my mates. “We all have come through at the same time and we have those connections, and I think a big thing with footy is being able to trust your teammates. If you already have something in place, there’s no real reason to kind of change that and switch it up. Treyvon is one of the most exciting talents in Australian rugby. World Rugby “So I think the friendships and the connections that I already have are also a big part of my reasoning to stay in Australian rugby.” The brothers spoke highly of their dealings with the Chiefs, but ultimately turned down the lucrative offer because they felt they have unfinished business in rugby together – and believe the money will follow them eventually.



“Obviously, it was exciting [to get the PNG offer] and yeah, we did meet with them, and I think that was probably both our first real kind interest from league. So we tested the waters and we were trying to see what it was all about,” Treyvon said. “But I think Rugby Australia had a lot to offer as well. Like I said before, loyalty played a big part in where we are now and that helped us to a decision on where we wanted to be for the next couple of years... “The money is going to come, it’s probably not the biggest worry at the moment. We need to focus on establishing ourselves in our respective teams.” Kadin said that beyond immediate financial rewards, rugby will offer the brothers a chance to travel the world while playing the game they love. “I love rugby union and the possibilities that it can bring with the worldwide game were a big thing for me to stay here,” Kadin said.



“To travel around the world, playing international teams – and even if it’s club level, you can go over somewhere like France. The possibilities of doing that sort of thing, you don’t get that in other sports.” The Ella brothers brought an almost telepathic understanding to the Wallabies back line in the 1980s and the Pritchards believe they can eventually replicate that synergy as a centre partnership for the Australian Test team. Kadin Pritchard dreams of forming a centre partnership with Treyvon at Test level for the Wallabies . Getty Images “It’s definitely a dream of ours to link up at some point,” Kadin said. “We’ve been separated for a reason: to build ourselves up in our own teams and build the groups around us. “By the time we get to the Wallabies, we’ll be set to go, because we’ve got that brother intuition ... we want to play together in the centres, with Trayvon at inside centre.



“It’s definitely been a thought in my mind becoming that 12 and 13, and you probably don’t see it too often having brothers in the centres with that connection. We’re just almost interlinked and we know how each other plays from doing it so often in the backyard.” Having spent endless hours playing together as kids, the two brothers came up against each other for the first time last season, when the Reds faced the Brumbies in Super Rugby. But Treyvon says it is when playing together on the same side that their close relationship brings an extra edge. “We probably don’t have to speak as much as other players would; we can communicate with our body language and trust is a big factor in the connection that we have over other players,” Treyvon said. At 22 years old, Kadin has always felt protective of Treyvon, who is three years younger than him. Treyvon affectionately calls Kadin the family’s “test dummy”, the older brother who had to forge the way into professional rugby before passing on the lessons learned along the way. Though separated by distance, the brothers still speak regularly and operate as a unit when it comes to making decisions on their rugby future.



The brothers have been brought up to support one another, wary that there will always be others outside the family who want to tear one or another of them down. “We know what each other can do and why should we hate on our family when you’ve got haters outside already,” Kadin said. “The tightness of our family, it’s just been brought through by our dad. Treyvon Pritchard suffered serious injuries in this hip drop tackle against Wales at the Junior World Championship, but is recovering well after surgery. Stan Sport “We’re our own biggest supporters, we’ve got to support each other and build each other up so there’s no hate coming from within, and we have a support group here. “There’s no way I’m going to hate on what my bro’s doing. I’m just going to hype him up to be the best player in the world. What’s the point of trying to pull him down when everybody else is trying to do that?”



Both brothers are currently recovering from injuries. Kadin is nursing a hamstring strain but hopes to return to play for the Brumbies in the Super Rugby AUS competition, while Treyvon is recovering from an operation after breaking his right leg ain a hip drop tackle while representing Australia Under 20s. Treyvon’s current recovery timeline is between 12 and 18 weeks. Related Article Australian rugby ‘Run us off our feet’: Wallabies’ surprising ploy to prepare for Japanese heat Both brothers are focused on establishing their positions with their respective Super Rugby clubs ahead of a new season, but Treyvon is aware there will always be future possibilities, whether in rugby or the NRL. “We’re definitely not closed off to playing overseas, and I think once we make a decision on that, I think we would probably look to play together, I don’t see why we wouldn’t,” Treyvon said. “I think living in a different country is hard enough, so I think being with the older bro would be awesome. “I’m [also] not closed off to the NRL. Obviously all the noise that’s been happening recently probably sparked a bit of interest for everyone, but it’s definitely an option down the track. I’m with the Reds for three years and with Aussie rugby for three years, so whatever happens after that happen.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil prices climb; BHP, CSL results ahead
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil prices climb; BHP, CSL results ahead Stan Choe Updated August 18, 2026 — 6:24am ,first published 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks edged further from their record heights on Monday after rising oil prices cranked up the pressure on inflation and financial markets. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent but remains near its all-time high set Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 272 points, or 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.3 per cent. Wall Street opened the week with more losses. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 6.04am AEST pointing to a fall of 40 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US71.03¢. Reporting season continues with BHP and CSL results slated to be released today. Wall Street’s losses solidified in the afternoon when oil prices accelerated upward. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 2.7 per cent to $US90.87.



Related Article Exclusive

James Packer James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares It’s been careening back and forth because of uncertainty about what the war with Iran will do to the global flow of crude. Last month alone, Brent zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. Monday’s rally for oil prices sent Treasury yields in the bond market higher, which in turn raised the pressure on the economy and prices for all kinds of investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 4.72 per cent from 4.68 per cent late Friday. It has shot up from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran, largely because higher oil prices are worsening inflation and upping the probability that the Federal Reserve will have to hike interest rates. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy. The average long-term US mortgage rate has already jumped near its highest level in a year because of the rise in the 10-year Treasury yield, though reports last week said that inflation in July was not as bad as earlier in the summer.



Usually around this time of year, anticipation is building on Wall Street to hear from the head of the Federal Reserve about where it may take interest rates. But the Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, may give little insight at this year’s economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of this month, according to Thierry Wizman, a strategist at Macquarie Group Warsh has been adamant about giving Wall Street less guidance about the Fed’s plans for interest rates. Wall Street has run to records despite high inflation in large part because profits are booming for U.S. companies. Those in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver growth of roughly 50 per cent for earnings per share in the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That’s much better than analysts expected and would be the best since five years ago, when the economy was erupting out of the chasm created by the COVID pandemic. Nearly all the companies in the S&P 500 have turned in their profit reports for the spring. Still to come are big retailers, including reports this week from Home Depot, Target and Walmart.



Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Trump makes America Inc’s grip on the world even tighter They’re facing pressure. Their customers’ incomes may be turning iffier after U.S. employers surprisingly cut more jobs last month than they added. At the same time, their customers are continuing to see bills rise quickly as inflation remains much higher than anyone would like. A report last week said that shoppers surprisingly spent less at U.S. retailers last month than in June, and CEOs for retailers could give color this week on what they’re seeing. On Wall Street, trading was relatively quiet Monday. L3Harris Technologies fell 4.6 per cent after the defense company said Christopher Kubasik stepped down as its CEO and chairman following “certain conduct by Kubasik that was not consistent with the values of the Company.” It gave few details but said the conduct was not related to its financial reporting, controls, customer relationships or operational performance.



Alphabet dipped 0.5 per cent even though Berkshire Hathaway said it increased its investment in Google’s parent company, along with several homebuilders. Berkshire built a reputation for buying stocks at affordable prices under its former CEO, famed investor Warren Buffett. Constellation Brands fell 6.2 per cent after Berkshire said it sold all its holdings in the seller of Modelo beer and Robert Mondavi wine. All told, the S&P 500 fell 40.70 points to 7,745.06. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 272.63 to 53,459.78, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 84.25 to 26,644.91. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped in Europe following a stronger finish in Asia. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7 per cent after a report said Japan’s economy grew at a slower pace in the April-June quarter than economists expected. Indexes jumped 1.3 per cent in Hong Kong and 1.4 per cent in Shanghai for some of the world’s biggest moves.
